speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: VANCOUVER HOTEL, VANCOUVER, AND EMPRESS HOTEL, VICTORIA  THREATENED STRIKES
speechtext: should like to address a question to the Minister of Labour. Can he assure the house that every effort is being made to avert threatened strikes of hotel employees at the Vancouver hotel, Vancouver, B.C., and at the Empress hotel, Victoria, B.C.?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: VANCOUVER HOTEL, VANCOUVER, AND EMPRESS HOTEL, VICTORIA  THREATENED STRIKES
speechtext:
The hon. member advised me that he intended to ask a question in regard to the employees of the Vancouver hotel at Vancouver and the Empress hotel at Victoria. In answering I will deal first with the situation at the Empress hotel at Victoria. There is a dispute as to the terms of a new collective bargaining agreement between the employees and the management of the hotel. This hotel, being operated by a private corporation, is under the jurisdiction of the provincial

government of British Columbia and I am informed that the usual conciliation services have been extended by that government. However, I am also informed that the dispute still exists and the representatives of the employees have notified the hotel management that the services of the employees will be withdrawn at midnight on June 3.
In regard to the Vancouver hotel at Vancouver the situation is somewhat different in that this hotel comes under the jurisdiction of the federal authorities because of the nature of its ownership. Here too the negotiations between the union and the management have failed to bring about a settlement of the terms of a new contract. On the recommendation of my officers I appointed a conciliation board following the failure of direct negotiations. Two members of the board made a majority report and the third member made a minority report.
Representatives of the employees have notified me that the provisions of the majority report are acceptable to the employees. The representatives of the management have the matter under consideration. This morning I was advised by the national vice-president of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees and Other Transport Workers that the employees will withdraw their services from the Vancouver hotel at midnight, June 3, 1952. I have some hope that the parties may reach an agreement before the time set for the strike.

I should like to address a question to the Minister of Public Works. What is the reason for the delay in removing the wreckage of the Burlington canal bridge?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The question of the cause of delay in replacing the Burlington canal bridge recently wrecked is one that necessitated having to give consideration to the problem from two different angles, first the permanent replacement and second the temporary replacement, in this case the location of the temporary replacement, which undoubtedly will have a bearing on the permanent replacement, had to be given consideration. We had to contact interested parties such as the department of highways and the Hamilton harbour commission.
The question of the removal of the wrecked bridge is one that had to be given consideration from the standpoint of whether it was to be scrapped or an attempt made to put
Inquiries of the Ministry it back in its original location. This required considerable investigation of contractors' proposals with relation to both projects.
In connection with the removal we contacted all local qualified contractors and it was necessary to give considerable study to the method suggested and the price asked by each. It was only yesterday that we received a proposal from a contractor whose methods were considered satisfactory and whose price was materially below that of any of the other proposals. A start is to be made within a week and it is anticipated that the wreck will be removed in from three to four weeks. Plans and specifications are now ready covering a temporary pile trestle for which tenders will be called immediately and we will be in a position to proceed with construction thereof on completion of the removal of the wreckage.

speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Defence Production. In view of recent press reports that there is a good chance for the early relaxation of controls on steel perhaps the minister would care to make a statement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RELAXATION OF CONTROLS
speechtext:
The difficulty about making any statement with regard to the relaxation of controls on steel arises from the fact that there is a possibility of a strike occurring in the steel industry in the United States. Aside from that there has been some easing in the supply of reinforcing steel and the regulations in that regard have been relaxed for buildings using only a small amount of that type of steel. Controls must be maintained as long as we require substantial imports from the United States under the controlled materials plan. There is no way in which Canadian users can qualify for imports from the United States except through the Department of Defence Production.
Supplies of structural steel and heavy steel plate are still difficult, probably as difficult as at any time in the last two years. Therefore, there is not much hope of relaxing the regulations in that regard until Canadian production comes in during the fourth quarter of 1952. We hope that then the situation of shortage will be materially eased.

I have no questions to raise in regard to this usual request, except that I would ask the minister whether the collections of government revenues up to the present time give any indication, as they did a year ago, of a surplus which eventually proved to be quite large. No, I have not the figures. In point of fact, Mr. Chairman, I was discussing the matter the other day with my deputy minister. We proposed, at one time, to issue the figures for the first two months. There will be some change in the way in which the figures will be presented in this respect. Last year I found that there appeared to be considerable misinterpretation and misunderstanding of the actual results arising out of the fact that the larger charges come in for inclusion in the figures in the latter part of the year. It seemed to me that a more accurate picture would be given from month to month of the public accounts if some of these annual charges could be pro-rated throughout the year. I asked the controller of the treasury to look into that question to see if it could not properly be done.
I understand it is going to be done, and the first statement which comes out will reflect that suggestion. On the first question the hon. member asked me I am informed, although I have not seen the detailed figures, that as usual the first month of the year will show a surplus, since a large part of the payments which are made in that month are charged against the previous year.
The minister, I take it, has not got these figures to give us at the moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
I am interested in the warning which the minister gave us, and which we have heard before. With deference, I would say that last year he was proven to be very wide of the mark.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We can also take it that, as usual, the various items provided in this bill, together with the items provided in the previous interim supply bill, do not in any case add up to twelve-twelfths?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

Before the resolution carries I should like to take this opportunity, if I may, to raise a question which I raised previously, and perhaps to amplify it slightly. The last time no answer was given, but I have no doubt that inadvertently the minister overlooked it. The question concerns the government use of the services of so many of our smaller business people, in both agriculture and industry, for the purpose of collecting government taxes. I raised the question before, and I raise it again now, to give the minister an opportunity of explaining that

situation. I was not raising it in any critical way, but it has been concerning me and I think it has concerned a good many .people that the government should be using so many people who can ill afford the expense to which they are put in the collection of government taxes.
I want to add to that another factor which has become more widespread than it used to be, because not only does the small fellow have to collect income taxes at the source for his two or three employees and keep an extra set of books in order to make accurate returns for the government, but in addition to that there is the question of sales taxes. In many instances the employer has to concern himself with these excise taxes as well as unemployment insurance, and it takes a great deal of .attention and causes a good deal of expense. On top of that, the bureau of statistics has walked in on the little businessman all over the country. I am not suggesting we should not have the information, but I am wondering whether or not all of that expense should be borne by the little fellows across the country who are having a difficult time to make ends meet.
I do not know whether the minister has seen the questionnaire sent out by the bureau, and I suppose he cannot be expected to look over every publication of the government, but if he does look at one he will find it is very intricate and difficult to answer. The questions not only include particulars about his business, but sometimes seem to go too far with respect to the information requested. All of these things have to be done at the expense of the little fellow, and I am wondering whether or not it is actually becoming discriminatory so far as our taxpayers are concerned. I should like to ask the minister for an explanation of that, but as I say I have not been unduly critical of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I apologize to the hon. member. He raised the question the other day and I had intended to .answer it but 1 overlooked doing so. I take it he is referring to the obligation which is imposed on employers, for instance, to deduct taxes at the source and remit them to the Receiver General of Canada. The short answer to his question is, of course, that that is one of the obligations of citizenship. Our tax structure is progressive. The smaller businessman pays a smaller tax, whether he operates as an individual or whether he operates in corporate form. In the case of a corporation a small business, as we know, has a lower tax rate than the larger one.
If the businessman or other employer who is required to deduct and remit these taxes
Interim Supply
were to be compensated for that, we would have to impose additional taxes in order to pay that compensation. Those taxes would have to fall on him. Since the obligation is rather widespread throughout the country, I must say that I had never thought there was any real inequity in imposing what, as I say, seems to me to be an obligation of citizenship imposed upon those who are engaged in business undertaking. To the best of my recollection my hon. friend is the first one, since I have been the Minister of Finance, who has raised the question in the terms in which he has raised it. I have heard individual taxpayers, chiefly large corporations, complain about the expense they are put to in order to deduct taxes on wages at the source, to remit sales tax and so on. Admittedly that requirement does involve extra accounting and overhead charges; but as I have pointed out to all those who have complained, if we did not do that we would have to increase substantially our overhead charges ourselves and impose taxes to pay for them. On balance I think the system which is in force today, and which resembles that in force in other countries which have tax systems similar to ours, is a substantially fair one.

I can understand the minister's point of view in that matter, but I think a halt must be called some time to the burden placed on people, particularly the little fellow in business, industry and agriculture. Year by year he is being loaded with further burdens. It is not only a question of collection of the income tax at the source but it also concerns other taxes and other reports, to the point that if you are going to be in business now-and nearly the same thing applies in agriculture-you have got to have some kind of accountant at your elbow in order to carry out the requirements and to meet the burdens that the government is imposing on you. I think a review should be made, either by the Department of Finance or by some other department, of the burdens which I have described and as to how they are actually affecting the little fellow across the country.
I am sure the government has not in mind discriminating in this matter. But on the other hand, unless somebody raises this question, this thing may go on to the point that it will become unbearable. I think now would be a good time for the government to call a halt on the burdens and the levies they are making in this way upon businesses generally, and to see whether or not some more simplified method can be found so that these

Interim Supply
people will not find the burden quite so heavy, both in the matter of expense and in work.
It is all very well for us here to adopt a big, high-level attitude about taxation and such things. But on the other hand, if you are in a little store, or on a farm, you have not all the facilities which government departments have to make these reports. It is one thing for somebody in an office in Ottawa to figure out some nice report that is to be made by somebody several thousand miles away; but that somebody is going to find it rather difficult, sometimes, to make that report especially without some assistance. I think a halt should be called before further burdens are imposed. I think a review ought to be made of the burdens that are at present in existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend can rest assured that we are constantly looking for ways to simplify and to improve our methods. May I assure him also that I share his concern about the little fellow.

Will the minister comment more specifically on that portion of the observations by the hon. member for Peel which related to the present activities of the dominion bureau of statistics which are increasing the obligations of many small businesses in the matter of making returns? We all regard the dominion bureau of statistics as a valuable governmental bureau; but in my experience, of late I have been receiving more complaints than previously about the multiplicity of returns which the bureau is requiring businesses to make. Does the minister care to comment specifically with regard to the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not too familiar with the detailed operations of the bureau of statistics. It may or may not be the case that they are asking for more returns than they need. My hon. friend is as fully aware as I am of the vital part that up-to-date and accurate statistics play in the conduct of modern business and modern government. The completion by businessmen and individuals of returns to the bureau of statistics is an obligation of citizenship such as that to which I referred in regard to tax deductions. I feel sure, however, that the remarks which he has made will be noted by the dominion statistician; I will see that they are brought to his attention. I am speaking broadly now, but I do not believe that the bureau of statistics is unreasonable with regard to the type of information which it asks for from the Canadian businessmen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
While we are on this general item which provides for one-twelfth of all

the estimates of all departments, there is a question which I should like briefly to put again to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I note that he is still in his place and perhaps he might deal with my question if he is in a position to do so. It relates to the matter which I raised yesterday on the orders of the day, namely the declaration of martial law in South Korea by Syngman Rhee.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said yesterday that he had received no official information and therefore felt that it was not proper for him to comment at that time. I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs knows why some of us are concerned about events there, and I am sure that he shares our concern. We all know that the United Nations went into Korea in support of the principle that there ought to be collective resistance to aggression. But happenings in South Korea do have a bearing on the morale of the nations involved in the Korean conflict, and it does seem that the principles of democracy are being rather flagrantly violated by Syngman Rhee.
As the minister indicated to me yesterday, there is a United Nations commission on the unification and rehabilitation of Korea which has made suggestions to the government there concerning democratic processes, but that is about as far as the minister's answer went yesterday. The matter is very much in the news. The reports from South Korea are exceedingly disturbing. I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs has had, since yesterday, any further report on the basis of which he might make a statement or whether he would comment on what attitude Canada takes toward this matter, and what the United Nations is doing about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before my colleague answers, Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I might raise this point? I am not sure whether or not it is in order, when we are in committee of supply, to discuss any question which may arise under the estimates. It may be that it is in order. I am not sufficiently expert in the rules to be sure whether it is or not. I have some doubts; but even if it is in order, I would hope that we do not embark upon general debate on interim supply. In my experience it has never been done when we are in committee. Some speeches have been made when the Speaker was in the chair, but not when we were in committee. I realize that we did not have to have a motion to go into committee of supply today; and for that reason I am not objecting to a reply being made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the question put by the

hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. But there are, of course, opportunities to ask such questions either on the orders of the day or when the estimates of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are under discussion. In any case, I am just appealing to the committee to try to keep the general debate down as much as possible and perhaps more strictly in line with expenditures rather than to discuss general questions of international affairs.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was not trying to take undue advantage of what I think to be our right on this item to discuss almost anything; but the fact is that we are being asked to vote one-twelfth of the items of the Department of External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is a question about which some of us are concerned. I had thought of repeating my question on the orders of the day today but since we were going into committee of supply, I thought it might be more suitable on both sides to ask it at this stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all right.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On this occasion I do not want to deal at any length with the point which has been raised by my hon. friend, which indeed he raised yesterday. The reason will, I am sure, commend itself to him. We have followed with interest and with concern the reports that have appeared about political developments in South Korea, because we have now a special concern with that part of the world.
But before making any statement on the matter I want to be quite sure-and I know the house would want me to be quite sure- that the reports in the press are accurate, in their essential particulars at least. Therefore we have been making inquiries through sources that are open to us-we have no diplomatic representative in Korea-and we hope to have a report on this matter shortly.
Press reports indicate, as hon. members know, that martial law has been declared in South Korea by the head of the government there, on the ground that communist activity in Pusan and in other places makes such a declaration desirable at this time. Hon. members also know that there is to be an election in Korea in July. The relationship between these two developments is not quite obvious at the moment, but there may be one. However, I would prefer not to say anything more about it until we get a more authoritative report than is before us now. The estimates of External Affairs will be
Interim Supply
before the house shortly and I may be in a position to make a longer statement on the subject at that time.

I want to add a word to what was said by the hon. member for Eglinton. No one has a higher appreciation of the bureau of statistics than I have, and yet, there is a danger that people who are expert and keen in what they are doing may just like to go on and on. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not oblivious of this, but I would like to feel also that perhaps the finance department is keeping an eye on these things, because unless they are strictly controlled they can go on and on to infinity.

speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that his remarks will be brought to the attention of the bureau of statistics; but I can also assure him that the finance department uses the material made available by the bureau of statistics to a very great extent.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Greenwood was asking some questions yesterday with regard to temporary employees of the Department of Justice. I have here some figures in relation to those employees.
The estimates provide for 44 temporaries, four of whom have been made permanent since the estimates were drawn up. Of the remaining 40, three are eligible for permanency and will likely be made permanent in due course. Eight are employed in the minister's office, and are not ordinarily eligible for permanent appointment. Eight are married women who after marriage remained on on a temporary basis, and are ineligible for permanency. Eight are not qualified for permanency because of a lack of the necessary service. Thirteen are not qualified for permanency because they have not qualified by examination.
I believe this accounts for all of them. The hon. member also raised the question as to the difference in their terms of employment. I am informed that these are the main differences:
Employees who are permanent are contributors under the Civil Service Superannuation Act, while the others whose terms of employment are on a temporary basis pay four per cent or five per cent of their salaries into the retirement fund. On leaving the

service members of the temporary class receive back the total of their contributions to this fund. Then, in the event of their later becoming permanent, the amount to their credit in the retirement fund is transferred, to make their pensions applicable as from the time at which they entered the temporary service.
The permanent employee, after ten years of service, may become eligible, depending upon the circumstances, to receive superannuation upon retirement. Incumbents of, for example, class 2 stenographers, temporary, or any other classified position, may be either temporary or permanent employees, and salaries and hours of work are identical in respect of both. The temporary employee, upon being certified in all other respects as permanent, has to pass the same health examination the permanent employees pass when they are appointed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
We will now proceed to item 175.
175. Administration of justice, miscellaneous expenditure, including expenses of litigated matters, $21,200.

Yesterday, just before six o'clock, I made reference, under this item, to the matter of the appointment of judges, and particularly to an article by the president of the Canadian Bar Association which appeared at page 28 of the Canadian Bar Review for January of this year. It was agreed there was not time enough to embark upon a discussion last night. I should like now, therefore, to return to this subject, to make some observations!, and to ask the minister if he would comment upon them and upon the article in general.
There is no cause to explain why members of the House of Commons, particularly those who are also members of the bar, should bring this matter up for discussion, particularly in the light of General Clark's very pertinent observations; because there is, as he points out and as I am sure the minister and most hon. members would agree, no matter of greater importance than to ensure that only men of the highest calibre should be appointed to positions on the bench.
I am not going to base my remarks in this connection solely upon accusations of improper practice by the present government. Indeed, if I were to do so I think the minister's answer would be to attempt to show that other governments have been as bad as this one-and probably he would say they have been worse. If the minister or anyone else were to make that answer, then my reply to him would be that two wrongs do not make a right. When we are discussing the maintenance of the independence of the judiciary,
Supply-Justice
and the necessity for high standards of qualification by those who are appointed to the bench-qualifications which should be quite removed from any question of political affiliation-it would be no answer to a criticism on that score to say that the practice had prevailed in the past, and that the standard of requirements had been lowered by other governments. To do so would be but to admit that a bad practice does exist at the present time.
Without going further on this tack, I think it cannot be denied that the vast majority, indeed practically all of the judges appointed in recent years, and for many years back, have been lawyers who, at the time of their appointments, held the same political affiliations as the party in power. To this extent there is justification for the warning frequently sounded in the house by the hon. member for Lake Centre, that we must never allow the condition to develop wherein the chief consideration in the matter of qualification for appointment to the judiciary is that of political fitness rather than legal attainments.
In this regard the remarks of General Clark, as contained in the article to which I have referred, are of particular interest. Since he is president of the Canadian Bar Association, in addition to being a lawyer of great eminence, his remarks are entitled to the serious consideration of the house.
I am going to take the liberty therefore of quoting quite extensively from his article, and particularly of emphasizing those points in it with which I agree. I should like to commence by reading a general statement of General Clark's to be found at page 30 of the Canadian Bar Review. It is as follows:
The support given by the bar of this country to the bench is traditional. The example of the bar has been emulated by the people as a whole. British justice is something we treasure. The history of the administration of justice in British countries has been such that it is the common belief of the people that the highest interests of the country are dependent, perhaps more dependent on the judiciary than on any other institution in our democracy.
That is a statement of the position with which I am quite certain we all agree. It seems to me the very statement of that principle indicates the supreme importance which must be attached to this question of maintaining the independence of the judiciary. After referring to the resolution dealing with this subject passed by the Canadian Bar Association at its annual meeting in 1949, General Clark goes on to refer to the position of a former very great prime minister of this country and) a very great lawyer, the late Lord Bennett. He points out that Lord Bennett himself had said that he found it extremely

Supply-Justice
difficult to follow the ideal that legal eminence and qualifications alone should be considered in making appointments to the bench. The late Mr. Bennett, as he then was, said that he deprecated the sort of political pressure that was sometimes applied with respect to this matter. After making that reference, the president of the bar association continues as follows, as reported on page 32 of this article:
I believe that the present Prime Minister, now the association's honorary president, and the president, and the Minister of Justice are likewise deeply convinced that the welfare of Canada demands that men of the highest character, and endowed with the best brains that can be found in the profession, should be selected in making appointments to the bench. I am satisfied that no prime minister or minister of justice has ever looked with equanimity upon pressure from the political machine and upon public service as a proper justification for a person who is being entrusted with the power of life and death over the subject. I can conceive of nothing more subversive to the interests of the state than that pressure from those concerned with political expediency and party loyalty should be the determining factor in appointments to the bench. I say with the deepest conviction that politicians would not dare to intervene in the way they do if the bar of Canada assumed the role of leader of public opinion in this regard, and I am convinced that the prime minister and minister of justice, of whatever party may be in office, will readily subscribe to this principle if the bar acts with determination.
I have included the last sentence of that quotation particularly for the reason that, as I will point out in a moment, I feel there is a twofold responsibility in this matter, first, that of the government, and,1 second, that of the bar itself. After making these general comments on the position in Canada and stating in effect what is indisputable, namely, that appointments to the bench in Canada have unfortunately in many cases been far from free from political considerations and implications, General Clark then goes on to refer to the situation in England. He has this to say:
I have made personal Inquiries regarding appointments to the bench in England. Some ten years ago a then English practitioner told me confidentially that he was giving serious consideration to a suggestion by the lord chancellor that he accept an appointment to the bench. He was wrestling with the offer because he wanted to continue in practice. I inquired why that should worry him, and he replied that it was a tradition at the bar of England that if a man was offered an appointment to the bench he accepted it and sacrificed the emoluments of practice. Since he had been a member of parliament on the opposite side of politics to the government of the day, I wondered why the lord chancellor would offer him an appointment.
I pause there to observe that that very comment of the president of the Canadian Bar Association, namely, "since he had been a member of parliament on the opposite side of politics to the government of the day, I wondered why the lord chancellor would

offer him an appointment", indicates how in general the practice-and the impression that is gained with respect to the practice-in Canada concerning appointments to the bench differs widely from that in England. General Clark went on to say:
He replied that political affiliations made no difference whatever in appointments to the bench and he went on to say that the lord chancellor kept close track of the qualifications of practising barristers and their suitability for judicial office; he could not recall an instance where an appointment could have been characterized as political.
Last summer when I was in England I made further inquiries of a source that was thoroughly familiar with appointments since 1946. X was informed that the then lord chancellor, Lord Jowitt, had since 1946 appointed 70 per cent of the judges of England and only one of them had belonged to his own political party. The lord chancellor had been heard to say that nothing would cause him greater embarrassment than the appointment of members of his own party to the bench. I inquired what would occur if political pressure were brought to bear on behalf of a prospective appointee. The answer was that it would be ignored.
It is undeniable that the position in this country is vastly different from that in England where on the basis of this information a Labour lord chancellor, who had appointed 70 per cent of the judges of England, had appointed only one from the ranks of his own political party. The answer to that situation cannot be found in the statement that there are not very many lawyers in England of eminent qualifications who subscribe to the Labour party because the fact is there are many. It is a fact most significant and worthy of comment as illustrating the impartiality and the high standard followed in that country that only one out of all these appointments made by Lord Jowitt was that of an individual who belonged to his own political party.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is that the kind of impartiality you are asking for in political appointments, where the government makes one from their own party and all others from the opposition?
Of course that is the sort of political comment I might have expected the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make at this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You got it then.

The point I am making, and which the minister obviously fails to appreciate, is that it speaks very highly of the system in England, and it certainly shows a degree of impartiality one would never expect from him or some others of his type in this government. In making these appointments only one was made from the membership of the party in power.

Will the hon. member
permit a question?
Yes.

I am quite familiar
with the quotations the hon. member for Kamloops has given with respect both to the situation that Lord Bennett found rather unpleasant-
Is this a question or is the hon. member merely wanting to state something?

I am going to ask a
question. I am also quite familiar-
Perhaps the hon. member would not mind coming to his question.
I will come smack bang right to it. General Clark was a member of this house for three parliaments.
I am sorry, I do not mind answering the hon. member's question but-
I am asking a question.
-I wish the hon. member would come to his question.
My question is this: If the technique-
Not "if", ask your question.

-as suggested by General Clark was adopted would we be sure that, if the Liberal party was out of power and the Conservative party was in power, they would follow the principle adopted by Lord Jowitt?

I was hoping that it would not be necessary to deal with too many questions of a political nature. If my hon. friend and others will restrain their impatience a little longer they will see that I am going to deal with the basis upon which selections to the bench should be made and which I think would be highly satisfactory to all parties. Therefore I shall put off answering my hon. friend's question until a little later because I think he will then find a satisfactory answer to the point which he has raised. But I can say this: I am confident that when the Conservative party is elected to power it will appoint lawyers to the bench only on the basis of their legal qualifications and fitness for the position in question. Whatever be the political party in whose ranks such men are to be found, the principle to be followed must be to appoint the man most qualified.
The inescapable implication of what is contained in this article and what we know from our observations is that unfortunately the desirable standards have not always been followed in this country. It seems to me that there are two considerations which we should keep in mind. First, the government should approach the problem of making appointments to the bench on an absolutely impartial 55704-170
Supply-Justice
basis and not have as their first consideration the political affiliation of the person to be appointed. I think that duty goes without saying.
The reasons for it, although they have always been urgent, are of extreme urgency at the present time in view of the fact that we have abolished appeals from the Supreme Court of Canada to the privy council. That fact is significant in many ways, perhaps the most significant being that the Supreme Court of Canada is now the final custodian of the constitution of Canada. As the minister knows, there are many divergent opinions as to the interpretation of the constitution, particularly sections 91 and 92. In view of the peculiar position of this country with different races, different languages and different minority interests, it would be nothing less than catastrophic if the decision of constitutional questions were to rest with judges whose appointment had been based on their political affiliations.
I hope no one will say that in the remarks I am making I am condemning the calibre of those who now constitute the courts of our country. I am simply making a statement of general principle. I think that the answer to that criticism, if it ever be made, will be found in what I shall have to say in just a few minutes. But I do want to point out that it was never more important to make certain that we maintain the independence and high calibre of those appointed to judicial office in this country. Not only is there a duty upon the government in this connection; there is also a duty upon the members of the bar which is the second consideration upon which I should like to hear the comments of the minister. I was particularly impressed by the statement of General Clark with reference to the attitude of members of the bar in England to this question, and I repeat one passage as follows:
It was a tradition at the bar of England that if a man was offered an appointment to the bench he accepted it and sacrificed the emoluments of practice.
That tradition and duty apparently is accepted by the bar of England and I think it is incumbent upon our bar to ponder seriously accepting the same responsibility. I cSn appreciate the desire of the minister, in bringing into effect the recent salary increases, to remove some of the obstacles which might otherwise be felt by members of the bar to exist in connection with the acceptance of this type of appointment.
There is one other consideration which I think is important, that is, the duty of the government not only to be impartial with respect to these appointments but to maintain the independence of the judiciary after

Supply-Justice
the appointments have been made. I am not going to go into this question in any detail except to repeat what has been said before, something to which I fully subscribe.
I think the minister and the government should avoid so far as possible-and I feel it should be possible to avoid it completely -the appointment of judges to commissions dealing with problems having a political implication.
I do not mean that you can divorce politics, that you can put them in a vacuum. I realize that many problems have political implications. However, I think the minister knows what I mean when I refer to problems having political implications. I refer to problems which by their very nature are subject to political controversy in the house and throughout the country. I am strongly of the opinion that the appointment of judges to commissions dealing with matters of that kind has a most unfortunate effect in lowering the esteem and regard in which our bench is held throughout the country.
There are just two thoughts to which I should like to refer in conclusion. May I refer first to the resolution of the bar association passed at Banff in 1949. I think it is here that the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard will find an answer to his question. In that year the Canadian Bar Association passed this resolution:
Whereas it is the desire of the profession that the best qualified members thereof be appointed to judicial positions,
Therefore be it resolved that the government of Canada be requested to consult with a committee consisting of the chief .justice of the province and the chief justice of the trial division and representatives of the benchers of the law society in the province mentioned before making any appointment to the bench for that province.
I should like to ask the minister to what extent that resolution has been followed in the appointments which have been made to the bench since the date of its adoption by the bar association. As I say, I think my hon. friend will find an answer to his question right there. I am urging that that recommendation be followed by the government in all appointments to the bench.
Of course it would be highly absurd for anyone to suggest that the only qualified lawyers for appointment to the bench would be those belonging to the opposition party, but the suggestion is just as absurd that the only lawyers qualified for appointment to the bench are members of the party in power. Surely the proper procedure to follow is to consult with those who are best able to know the qualifications of persons in the province in question, that is, members of the bench of the province and benchers of the law society. Then, having consulted

with them, having taken their recommendations, let political considerations be left out of the picture entirely. I am not going so far as to say for a moment that any government should be criticized simply because it appoints to the bench a member who happens to support that government. To put the appointment beyond criticism, however, surely it is not too much to ask that before the appointment is made the opinion of those best qualified to know should be sought. This is not to suggest, either, that the government should abdicate its responsibilities in the matter. The responsibility for the final decision will rest just as squarely on the government under that system as it does now. All we are asking is that the government receive these recommendations and give consideration to them, rather than give greater weight, as appears to have been done sometimes in the past, to political considerations.
The other principal thought that I should like to leave with the committee and with the minister is this. Towards the conclusion of his article, General Clark said this, as found at page 34:
What are the practical steps towards the objective I have outlined, that is the objective of appointment to the bench being entirely impartial? First and foremost is the creation of a tradition within the bar of Canada that it is the duty of the practitioner to accept judicial appointments when offered. Could such a tradition be created in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How can you force an appointment on a man who does not want it?

I am sorry that a man who is a lawyer himself should have so completely missed the point of my remarks. If he has, perhaps my remarks have not been expressed too clearly. If he has found my remarks difficult to follow, I suggest that he read the article by General Clark. No one is suggesting that anyone could be forced from without to accept an appointment. The whole point of the remark is that there should be a tradition in the bar of Canada which, of itself, would compel the person to whom it is offered to accept it. For the benefit of the hon. member who interrupted, I am going to read this passage again.
First and foremost is the creation of a tradition within the bar of Canada that it is the duty of a practitioner to accept a judicial appointment if it is offered. Could such a tradition be created in Canada? I believe so. It exists in Great Britain. There, a man can refuse an offer once, but if he declines a second time it is my understanding that the appointment is not offered again and that he is left with the feeling that he has failed to recognize and live up to an important tradition.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That tradition exists here too.
It is a different kind of tradition, though.
I recall that we in this house have heard the Minister of Justice speak of the difficulty he has had in persuading lawyers to accept appointments.
Not the third time or the second time.

He was not speaking of the difficulty of persuading Conservative lawyers to accept an appointment either, or Liberal lawyers but lawyers in general. Out of the words of the Minister of Justice himself, the Minister of Public Works will get his answer. I believe that is one of the prime difficulties standing in the way of this matter of impartiality. I want to be fair in this matter, and it is for that reason I have been at pains to suggest that in my view there is a twofold responsibility. There is a responsibility resting upon the government to be impartial in their choice of appointments to the judiciary. Then, the bar, together with the bench, should be consulted and should assist in making it possible for impartiality to be shown and to enable the best man to be appointed by building up a tradition within its own ranks that appointment to the bench is not only an honour to the person appointed, but that acceptance of the offer is incumbent upon every member of the profession, because only by doing so can a lawyer really live up to the oath which he took at the time of his call of admission, the oath to maintain the best traditions of his profession and to preserve and further the interests of his country and of his monarch.

There are a few remarks I should like to make in view of the very able address to which I have just listened by the hon. member for Kamloops. I think it was a very idealistic speech, and it is possible that, from a theoretical point of view, what he suggests would be quite desirable. However, I would suggest that his ideals do not conform entirely with the facts. While he has assured us he believes that his own party would make appointments from that point of view, I wonder if he can tell me how many Liberal magistrates have been appointed in Ontario since the Conservative party has been in power? If any have been appointed, it is beyond my knowledge, and possibly they did not know what his politics were.
I am not suggesting that what he has said would not be a desirable tradition, but I say it would not work. I am not suggesting that appointments by the Minister of Justice is the finest method that can be devised;
55704-170 i
