obviously, mistakes could be made. But I know of no other system which would work in this country. 1 cannot conceive, for instance, of having appointments made or abetted by the law society of Upper Canada. I do not see how that gets rid of politics. The people who are benchers do not completely divorce themselves from politics because they are benchers. I have received many letters in the past from people who were running for office as benchers asking my support in their election.

But not on
the grounds of your politics.

On the ground that they are running for office. I do not follow, either, why that would divorce the thing from politics. Similarly, I do not feel that the bar association is in a position to select or approve those candidates. I do not see that their knowledge is any greater than-I do not think it is as great as-that of the Minister of Justice. I was at that meeting where the resolution was passed. While it was passed unanimously, a very small percentage of the bar of Canada was in attendance. My recollection is that there were only about 25 in the room at the time the resolution was passed. I do not think it can be regarded as something that represented the inclinations or desires of every member of the profession.
What is happening in England is perhaps a very suitable system for England. 1 do not think that because something happens in England it necessarily happens here. They have other customs, other traditions, and this is not England. 1 am very fond of England, as I know many of the members here are, but I am much fonder of Canada. 1 think that Canada is a distinct country which will establish its own traditions. It has done so in the past and will continue to do so in the future. The only point I am trying to make, Mr. Chairman, is that while I would hesitate to criticize the hon. member for Kamloops for suggesting this idealistic measure, I do not think that as a matter of practice it would function in this country at all. I think it would be quite impractical. I do not think it would achieve what he hopes it would achieve.
My observation of the appointments that are made is that they are of a very high calibre. I do not know any judges who have been appointed since I have been here whom I would criticize in the sense that they did not have sufficient legal standing or that they were not competent to carry out then-duties. From my knowledge of the minister, I

Supply-Justice
am quite sure that when future appointments are made they will be of the same high calibre.
You might be one of them yourself.

I am not suggesting that I should be one.
The point I am making is this. I think that the inherent defects, from a theoretical point of view, are more than compensated for by the fact that from a practical point of view the system has worked, that we have good judges, and that we have ended up with a high-calibre bench. While I like to listen to the suggestions of the hon. member for Kamloops on the subject, I believe that in practice they would not work.
Mr. Chairman, following up the remarks of the last speaker-
This is on the subject of judges.

Who are you to judge? The Good Book says: Judge not, that ye be not judged. Following up the remarks of the last speaker, who referred to magistrates and appointments in the province of Ontario, I should like to ask if he knows of one magistrate who went out when the Conservative government came into power following the Liberal government of Mr. Hepburn, when the whole province was loaded with Liberals? Not one of them was let out. They all held their jobs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; they did not.

I am not talking to you. Judge not, that ye be not judged. You look after your own Ottawa, redistribution and a lot of other things. X should like to ask the minister one question. Is he going to appoint Walter Thomson, of the late Liberal party in the province of Ontario, to a judgeship in Peterborough which he is looking for?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What do you think?

Do not forget that I said, "the late Liberal party". He was talking about lawyers in the province of Ontario receiving judgeships. According to the last vote, if there is any lawyer in Ontario who is not mixed up with politics in connection with one party or another, there are not many left that are Liberal; at least, they do not admit it if they are.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter is of such great importance that, before the item is passed, I think it is really essential that I

should say something concerning it. I am indeed indebted to the hon. member for Kamloops for having raised the matter. I had previously read in the Canadian Bar Review the report of the address of General Clark to the Edmonton section of the Canadian Bar Association upon this subject.
The Alberta section.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Knowing General Clark and respecting him as I do, I had hoped that I might have the opportunity of discussing with him the remarks which he had made before it might become necessary for me to reply publicly to them. Perhaps it is all for the best, however, that the hon. member for Kamloops has made necessary that reply today, because there is no gainsaying the truth of the passage which he quoted from General Clark's speech concerning the great importance of the judiciary in our democratic system of government. As one can see from the remarks of the last speaker, this is a topic which rather tempts some into political partisanship. The whole case of General Clark and of the hon. member for Kamloops is that political partisanship has played an inordinate part in the appointment of judges in this country. That being so, I want to do my very best today to treat of this partisan subject in a manner which will be as nonpartisan as I can possibly make it.
The hon. member for Kamloops has made a selection of excerpts from the speech of General Clark which are excellent, as far as they go, but which if I may say so, are not quite a complete cross-section. I should like to deal not only with those which he has mentioned but also with certain others that I think are relevant to this matter, for General Clark's statement is one which deserves a serious reply; and perhaps as suitable an official as any to make that reply is myself.
General Clark's central thesis is that our system of judicial appointments in this country is unworthy; and he makes it quite clear that its unworthiness consists in that the recommendations of members of parliament belonging to the party in office are given far too great weight in the making of such appointments. In support of that thesis he cites certain facts, to which I shall refer as I go along, and the probative value of which I question. He supports the Canadian Bar Association resolution which the hon. member for Kamloops has just quoted, namely:
Therefore be it resolved that the government of Canada be requested to consult with a committee consisting of the chief justice of the province and the chief justice of the trial division and representatives of the benchers of the law society in the province mentioned before making any appointment to the bench of that province.

The hon. member lor Kamloops has pointed up this resolution by suggesting that not only should they be consulted but that their recommendation should be taken.
The first point that I make in that connection is that by section 96 of the British North America Act it is provided that, and I quote:
The governor general shall appoint the judges of the superior, district, and county courts in each province . . .
Under the constitution that we have in this country the governor general always acts upon the advice of his responsible ministers, and these do not include the chief justices or law society benchers who, indeed, are occupied in discharging an entirely distinct function of government from the executive, namely, the judicial function.
The general trend of General Clark's speech is that the legal profession, acting through the law society in a manner which I think it may be fairly said that he does not too clearly delineate, should influence public opinion in this matter to devise a formula under which the control of the selection of judges would to a greater or lesser degree be influenced by if not vested in the chief justices and the benchers of the law society.
I take issue with General Clark and with the hon. member for Kamloops in this matter upon the ground that our constitution places the full responsibility for making appointments on the government, acting solely on the advice of its responsible ministers; and that this responsibility, in my view, should not be delegated or watered down by official and formal consultation with chief justices or representatives of the bar who, in this connection, constitutionally and politically, are not responsible to anyone.
In saying that, I do not intend to say or imply that we should not consult judges and members of the bar in connection with judicial appointments. As a matter of fact, ever since I have had the honour to be Minister of Justice I have continually consulted with individual members of the bars of the various provinces, with judges and, in certain cases, with chief justices concerning the suitability of such candidates as we had under consideration, just as I consult with members of parliament and with Canadian citizens generally who I think have something to contribute upon this same subject.
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, surely.

With regard to the minister's reference to consultation with members of parliament, may I ask whether the minister has ever consulted, in connection with the
Supply-Justice
matter which he is now discussing, any member of parliament other than a member of his own party?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the suitability of candidates, yes. Our purpose in consultation in the appointment of judges is to find out in a specific case whether, we will say, John Doe whose appointment we are considering is a good counsel; whether he is of good character; whether he is a good citizen; in a word, whether he possesses those qualifications which any judge should have; and I can assure my hon. friend that if he has been engaged in legal work in the courts, a lawyer who may belong to the Conservative party may be in the best position of all to appraise the legal ability of the candidate for judicial appointment.
I deprecate this contention that representations made by members of parliament in this connection should not be seriously considered. I think it is a sign of political immaturity, which is gradually disappearing, and at an increasing rate of late years, that the submission should be made that a person who has enjoyed the confidence of his fellow citizens to the extent that they have elected him to represent them in parliament should not be trusted to express a disinterested and intelligent opinion concerning the qualifications of other persons for judicial or other office.
In discussing these issues, let me admit at once-and in this respect I agree with General Clark, and with the hon. member for Kamloops, although I do not by any means go anything like as far as they do in that direction-that the present system of appointing our judges is not perfect. But I do contend that whether under Conservative governments or under Liberal governments our present system is very much better than any person hearing General Clark's speech, or listening to my hon. friend, the hon. member for Kamloops this afternoon, would ever think that it was.
Indeed, this very point can be inferred from a careful reading of General Clark's own statement. He refers, and quite properly, to the great prestige which the bench of Canada enjoys today. The hon. member for Kamloops likewise referred to that prestige. General Clark puts it this way.
Were it not for the fact that our profession is composed largely of men of character, integrity and ability, it would have been impossible for the bench of Canada to have achieved that prestige
Now, sir, I grant at once-as a lawyer I have no difficulty in doing so-the character, the integrity and the ability of our profession. But I do suggest at the same time that if the method of judicial appointment in Canada

Supply-Justice
were as bad as General Clark and the hon. member for Kamloops think and say that it is, then it would1 be most unlikely indeed for the bench of Canada to have enjoyed its present prestige, even in the face of the great integrity, character and ability of our legal profession; for according to General Clark, and I think according to the hon. member for Kamloops, the appointments to the bench are hot made upon the basis of character, integrity and ability but are determined largely by considerations, to use the language which was quoted this afternoon, of political expediency and party loyalty, which are the determining factors in the appointments to the bench.
General Clark, in a selection from his remarks that the hon. member for Kamloops chose not to quote, said that he had been a member of parliament himself and he knew the system well. Well, sir, I have been in public life for 25 years now, and during that time, in the dual capacity of a lawyer and a politician, I have made a few suggestions, not many, concerning the appointment of judges. I can honestly say that when I made those to the then minister of justice I thought and intended that I was making those recommendations and suggestions on the basis of merit. Some of them, I am sorry to say, were ignored. In other cases, the man whom I recommended was appointed, although I do not know whether it was on my recommendation. But in those cases in which the appointments were made, I do not know of a single instance in which the judge concerned did not give an excellent account of himself. Yet according to the thesis which has been developed this afternoon, I possessed excellent qualifications as a lawyer to make that recommendation, but as a politician my disqualification for making those recommendations would cancel out my qualification as a lawyer. That is the thesis we are asked to accept.
During the past three and a half years I have been in a position in which General Clark's alleged abuses, if they existed in fact, would have unavoidably come to my attention. I cannot agree, sir, for one moment that the impressions which General Clark formed as a member of parliament himself are accurate at the present time. In fact I know that his impressions are not accurate as of present conditions. Yet I applaud his good faith and the propriety of his making his speech; for these are matters which, in the public interest, should be discussed with the candour with which he has discussed them, and with which the hon. member for Kamloops has discussed them this afternoon, and with which I shall endeavour to discuss them.
General Clark referred, as did the hon. member for Kamloops, to the late Prime Minister Bennett's desire to make judicial appointments upon the basis of merit alone, and to the observation of Mr. Bennett's secretary, Mr. MacLean-and I quote:
That while Mr. Bennett would like to make merit the chief consideration he had found instead that party, race, religion, occupation and geographic location of the nominee are more important than his qualifications. He (the Right Honourable Mr. Bennett) dislikes this deference to political sentiment, and he has said so repeatedly. Appointments made by the party for party reasons are anathema to him. He wants a man of integrity, of capacity, and if such a man happens to be a political enemy, that makes no difference.
My comment upon these idealistic observations is that if a comparison were made between the number of Liberals appointed during the period from 1930 to 1935 when the Bennett government was in power with the number of Conservatives appointed during the period 1935 to 1940 when the Liberal government was in power it will probably be found-I have not bothered to make such a count because I do not engage in invidious comparisons of that sort

that the percentage in each case was fairly uniform. I am rather inclined to think that it would favour the probity of our party, but maybe that is a bias on my part. It would be fairly uniform and would constitute perhaps the best available argument in support of General Clark's thesis.
Yet I suggest-and is this not the point -that it would be a very grave mistake indeed to suppose, because a Conservative government tends to appoint Conservative lawyers and a Liberal government Liberal lawyers to the bench, that such appointments are made in disregard of merit. To hear some professing democrats talk one would think that it was a great disgrace to be a member of parliament, a defeated candidate, or to be affiliated with any political party, or to take any part whatever in democratic government; and that he who did any of these things had to abandon all claim to integrity, to ability or to character. Everyone knows that that is not true. Yet from surprising sources we hear arguments which seem to be based mainly upon this premise-we heard one this afternoon.
So far as race, religion and geographical location are concerned, it is only too clear that we in Canada have always had to face, and we have to continue to face, the fact of race and the fact of religion and the fact of geographical location of at least five separate and distinct economic areas in this country with several mutually conflicting interests. Now, facing these facts, what are we going to do? Are we going to plunge

our heads in the sand, and attempt to ignore them? Of course not; we have to make our Canadian democratic system work in the face of them. And in this connection it seems to me quite idle to hold up to us the example of a more homogeneous society under totally different conditions in Great Britain. I must confess that as a Canadian I am sometimes a little impatient with these examples of the superior wisdom and capacity in Great Britain which we are urged to emulate. For, on the whole, I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we Canadians have done not too badly at all, even when as in many cases we did not emulate these examples. Upon the whole the facts of race, religion and geographical location have been, under all governments in Canada, wisely and efficiently faced. This matter of judicial appointments is only one field in which they have been faced. They have been faced in many others. I would like to know in what countries in the world

 no country excluded-problems of race and language and conflicting economic interests have been more efficiently and wisely faced, with less violence and bad feeling, and with more harmony and unity than right here in Canada. I am not drawing any invidious comparisons. I am rejecting invidious comparisons; and saying simply that, under all the circumstances, quite a good job has been done in Canada by all governments facing these facts.
But I think, if I might say so, that it is an error to mix up this quotation which has been used by General Clark, and again by the hon. member for Kamloops, concerning these racial, religious and economic facts of life in Canada, with the political appointment of judges.
Let us examine the appointment of judges and see the extent to which political expediency and party loyalty are, not just factors, but determining factors in making them.
I suggest that what has happened in Canada through the years is that the party in power in Canada has appointed to the bench men who, for the most part, were men of high character and ability, most, but not all, of whom were not active in public life.
The result has been, with few exceptions, the excellent bench to which the hon. member for Kamloops has referred this afternoon. Judges sometimes, of course-individual cases -have proved unsuitable. But I suggest that where this is found to be the case, in the great majority of instances it is not because they, before appointment, belonged to this political party or that political party, but because they developed after appointment characteristics which no one, except those
Supply-Justice
who are habitually wise after the event, could have claimed they had before the appointment was made.
It is true, unfortunately, that in the appointment and conduct of human beings, whether as judges or as other office holders, there is always the unavoidable element of human fallibility and perversity; and there is in a small minority of cases a tendency of human beings when appointed to any position in which there is great security of tenure to act in a different manner from that in which they acted when they did not enjoy that security.
But I think in the interests of adding a little proportion to this picture which has been drawn by General Clark and by the hon. member for Kamloops, and in the interests of truth, I should point out that our party when in power is not in the position of having appointed to the bench no one but Liberals. Federal Liberal governments of this country have appointed men of such outstanding ability as Mr. Justice Locke, Mr. Justice Cartwright, and the late Mr. Justice Newcombe, all of the Supreme Court of Canada, who consider these constitutional questions which the hon. member for Kamloops says-and says correctly-are of such importance. Then, there is Chief Justice Williams of the court of queen's bench, Manitoba; associate chief Justice Tyndale of the superior court of Quebec; Judge Lord of the county court of Vancouver; and we have promoted outstanding judges such as Mr. Justice Montague of the court of appeals of Manitoba, Mr. Justice Keiller Mackay of the court of appeal of the province of Ontario. All these fine jurists, at that time in their lives when they were able to have political affiliations, so far as I know were not members of the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And Mr. Justice Gagne?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; and Mr. Justice Gagne of Quebec. I wish to assure my hon. friend, the hon. member for Kamloops, as well as General Clark himself who, I understand, is a Conservative in politics, that I am not mentioning these appointments by way of an invidious comparison, nor am I inviting a comparison; but simply in order to present a balanced picture to hon. members and to those to whose attention these remarks may come.
Has the minister before him at the moment the figure showing the total number of judges appointed by this government during its tenure of office?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I have not.

It would be interesting to have that figure.

Supply-Justice

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not a question of mathematics.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to deal with certain of the specific points General Clark makes. He says:
Men in public life, on the other hand, are subject to pressure from party organizers on this and other subjects.
Well, I am sure all of us are aware that men in public life are subject to pressure from a great many sources. If they have not the capacity for resisting pressure, then they should not assume positions of responsibility in public life. But I should like to put on record this assertion, that to imply, as General Clark has done, that pressure of party organizers has any important or even significant influence in the appointment of judges, is quite contrary to the facts, in my experience.
The minister has referred to "party organizers". Would he amplify the statement for our understanding. Does he include all party forces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was coming to that point. The term "party organizers" was the one General Clark used. As a matter of fact, when I first read that article I stopped to think about his statement, and 1 could not recall a single occasion upon which a party organizer had ever spoken to me on this subject.
The hon. member for Eglinton has asked me to develop that point. It is true that I have been approached on a number of occasions by members of the House of Commons-and, on occasion, by members of more than one party-concerning appointments; and very properly so. There is no reason why I should not be approached concerning the appointment of judges. It is equally true that I have taken the initiative to consult members of the house on a number of occasions concerning the capabilities of men being considered for such appointments. In these cases in which I spoke to members, I did so because I thought they would be able to speak authoritatively concerning the qualifications of a candidate. But it will leave the wrong impression upon hon. members in the committee if I do not hasten to emphasize the fact that the great majority of those conversations were concerned primarily with the ability of the candidate in question to serve as a judge.
General Clark quotes for a Vancouver newspaper a report from Ottawa, as follows:
Members of the House of Commons were astonished that a stranger was in line for a possible vacancy on the bench. They were also represented to have been dissatisfied with the appointment of a certain lawyer who had never been active in politics . . .
tMr. Fulton.1
Presumably this concerns my actions as Minister of Justice-and that-
. . . fears were increased because of recent nonpolitical appointments in Ontario, where it was getting around that judicial appointments were being made in a strange way. A special caucus of members was called in consequence and the Minister of Justice was approached to find out what was going on.
The first point I make in that connection is that in a matter of this importance a newspaper article of the type referred to is not a very satisfactory source of information upon which to base a definitive article or speech. I have not seen the newspaper article in question, but in relation to General Clark's statement I think I should say that no special or other caucus of members has ever made any representations to me upon the subject of judicial appointments. There may have been such a caucus, but if so its existence has never come to my attention. Any conclusions of that caucus that may have come to me certainly never came from any member or group of members representing a caucus.
The fact is that the reference in General Clark's speech to this special caucus of members was the first and only time I knew that any person was alleging that such a caucus existed. I think, however, I can identify correctly the reference to my recommendation for appointment as a judge of a certain lawyer who had never been active in politics, and to whom General Clark, quoting this Vancouver newspaper report, apparently has referred in his speech. If I do identify this case correctly it is a very fair sample of the method of appointment of the Department of Justice.
In that case what happened was that I had recommendations from lawyers, judges, members of parliament and other citizens concerning three lawyers. I gathered that two of these lawyers had been active in politics and that the third man was not in a position to be active, and had not been.
I considered all these representations and recommended the appointment of the third man, the non-active man, not because he had not taken any part in politics or because the other men had taken part but because of the three under consideration I thought the man who had not taken part was by long odds the best qualified for the appointment. In fact I was told quite pointedly that the members who had recommended the other two were quite displeased with this appointment, but so far as I know no one has ever suggested before or since that the man who was appointed was not eminently well qualified for the job or that he is not discharging his duties properly.

General Clark makes another point which concerns members of the house. He says:
Is it not unthinkable then that members of parliament who are not lawyers should consider it their perquisite to select and recommend men who are to occupy these highest of high offices?
1 must say from my experience that the implications of this question are exceedingly unfair and incorrect with regard to any members of parliament with whom I have had any contact. I have yet to meet a member of parliament who considered that it was his perquisite to select and recommend men who were to occupy judicial positions.
This is often the position in which a member is placed. Lawyers as a group are more than usually influential men in their community. Sometimes when they or their friends have rendered political favours to members of parliament they ask the members of parliament in turn to recommend them for judicial appointment. I would say it is very difficult in a case of that sort for the member to turn down the request. But my experience has been that where such a recommendation is made and I suspect the background of the recommendation, look the member in the eye and ask him point blank as to his opinion of the lawyer's competence and standing in the community, so far as I know I always get-I may be naive and have been led astray-within the limits of the member's knowledge in the matter, accurate and candid answers.
Moreover, on a number of occasions members of parliament, animated so far as I can see by no other interest than to get the best possible judge to fill a judicial post which has opened up in their community, have come to me with recommendations made on the basis of merit only. How do I know they were on the basis of merit only? Because I checked them with members of the bench and with colleagues at the bar of the candidate and confirmed that what the member had told me was true. I would not suggest for a minute that political considerations are not sometimes a factor, but they are not, in any case which has come to my attention, a determining factor.
There have been-and I think this point was raised one time by the hon. member for Macleod, who is not here today-a number of men appointed to the bench who have had experience in public life. The number is not large but there are some. I want to say that I make no apologies for these appointments. I think the men who were so appointed were men of ability, integrity and character notwithstanding that they had taken part in public life, and I entirely agree with General Clark's contention, with which I am sure the hon. member for Kamloops i55704-171
Supply-Justice
would also agree, that public service can be and is an important qualification for appointment to the bench.
In support of this contention I should like to quote an opinion expressed in his autobiography by a highly qualified expert. This man was one-indeed I do not know offhand of any other-who achieved his pre-eminence not only as an advocate, and as a member of the British House of Commons, and as one of the greatest ministers of the crown who ever held office in the United Kingdom, but also as a great law lord. Lord Haldane says in his autobiography at page 69:
I wish to record my strong conviction that, at all events, for a judge who is to sit in the supreme tribunals of the empire, and particularly in the privy council, a House of Commons training is a real advantage. One learns there the nuances of the constitution, and phases of individual and social political life which are invaluable in checking the danger of abstractness in mental outlook. I myself was peculiarly in need of such training, and I am thankful to have had twenty-five years of the great university of public life.
The bar has its uses as a training for the House of Commons, but it is not really a good school. The outlook in the house is very different from the outlook in the courts. If less scientific about details, the House of Commons' mind is wider.
This will give some comfort to the laity here.
I am not sure that a first-rate minister, although untrained as a lawyer, does not bring in a great legal bill better and more effectively than the best trained legal mind, unless that mind has, what is rare, the political gift by nature in a high degree.
Why is the minister going to England for his precedent this time?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He goes on to say:
The atmosphere is quite different. I remember once arguing a case in the court of appeal before Lord Esher and Lord Justice Rigby.
Lord Justice Rigby, an old and valued friend of mine, had entered the House of Commons late in life. He never quite understood its ways, and was not appreciated to the extent which his sterling qualities of a non-political kind warranted. I was opening an appeal on the construction of an act of parliament, and I was arguing that the statute must be read as a whole in order to collect from within its four corners what I called the "mind" of the legislature in the controlling purpose which the sections indicated. "Mind of the legislature", cried out Lord Esher to me from the bench, "and you, Mr. Haldane, have been twenty years in the House of Commons and yet speak of it." "Yes," thundered out Lord Justice Rigby, "and the House of Commons is a place where if a man talks sense they call him a lawyer". Notwithstanding this, law and politics may go better together than some people think . . .
I should like to deal now with an important matter which has been touched upon by two preceding speakers and by General Clark. General Clark refers to the merits of the British system of judicial appointments when he says that it is a tradition at the bar of England that if a man

Supply-Justice
is offered an appointment to the bench he accepts it and sacrifices the emoluments of practice.
I admit that the hon. member for Kamloops was right in his statement this afternoon that sometimes when we ask lawyers in Canada to go on the bench we are told they cannot consider the acceptance of such an appointment. For example, in the case of a vacancy not so long ago we approached four lawyers who refused the judicial appointment before the one who accepted it.
Before we make any comparisons between the English and Canadian barristers in this regard however I think we should look a little beneath the surface at some of the relevant facts. For instance, when General Clark refers to cases where English barristers have thrown away incomes of $200,000 a year to accept a judicial appointment paying I believe $20,000, it sounds quite impressive until we recollect the difference of the net amount of income after income tax between $200,000 received at the bar and $20,000 received on the bench. On a mathematical basis, that difference is $180,000 a year, but after tax it amounts to only $7,500 per year.
The minister will admit that that is a fairly recent development in England and General Clark's statement was not confined to recent years.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite right, but I am speaking about the present situation, about the period in my own knowledge. In Canada the difference is not $7,500, it is $43,000. In both cases the example is that of a married man without dependents.
Who is this mythical creature who earns $200,000 a year.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are some barristers in England earning that.
But not in Canada.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There may not be plenty in Canada, but there perhaps are a few. Having dealt with them in respect to this very matter I can say from direct knowledge that Canadian barristers are not any more mercenary in their attitude toward these appointments than are the English barristers. I would say that two-thirds of the appointments made to the high courts during my time have involved the lawyers accepting them in diminution in income.

However
true that may be, and I am glad to hear that it is true, would the minister not agree that we have not reached the stage which apparently they have reached in England, where it is regarded to be a matter of duty

which is accepted by the best lawyers and where the minister would not run into such a case as he mentioned a moment ago where it was only the fifth man who took the appointment.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend by his question has very astutely anticipated the point I was going to make. Take the typical case of a man-I have had this experience- who is quite philosophical about accepting a diminution in income. The hon. member for Greenwood will remember that I developed this point when I was urging an increase in the salaries of judges. Like Mr. Micawber, except it is not a penny in this case, if a man's irreducible obligations are of the order of $30,000 a year and he has an income at the bar of $32,000 a year, the price of his accepting an appointment to the bench would be bankruptcy. As a matter of arithmetic it would be bankruptcy. Notwithstanding what we are told about the British bar, I cannot believe that members of the British bar who might be in that position would take on bankruptcy any more readily than would members of the Canadian bar.	.
I have had cases where highly qualified counsel have said, "I am sorry I cannot bridge this gap now; I have obligations to meet. I think in the course of a few years I will be free of my present obligations and the minute I am free I shall be delighted to go on the bench if the government is prepared to consider my appointment at that time." In such cases I. do not think the Canadian barristers need to take second place to the British barristers. We do not hear about cases in England where that happens.
A good deal of the criticism of Canadian judicial appointments seems to assume that the only reason why a number of eminent lawyers are still at the bar and not on the bench is that they have been passed over in favour of those with greater political influence. Whereas, for the reasons I have stated-this is particularly so in the larger cities-the fact is that there are quite a number of highly placed members of the bar who have been forced to refuse judicial appointments.
The tenor of my remarks is not that political influences are entirely absent but that they are definitely not of a dominating character and are brought to bear much less frequently and are of less potency than General Clark seems to think. Certainly we would welcome greater interest in this matter by the Canadian Bar Association or the bench or the bar of Canada, but that does not mean that we can abdicate in favour of any such

body our constitutional responsibility to appoint judges. Indeed I feel pretty certain that the great body of Canadian citizens would not want us to indulge in any such abdication.
That we must answer the criticism of professional opinion goes without saying, but the question in all these cases is whether the appointment of a lawyer whom we select is a better appointment than the appointment of other then available and willing members of the bar. On that basis I am prepared to defend any appointments I have recommended.

I think a service has been done this afternoon by the hon. member for Kamloops in raising this question which has had extended discussion. I do not propose to labour the subject at any length, but I would not wish the impression created by the remarks of the Minister of Justice to pass without some observations of a corrective nature.
In the first place, if we heard only the remarks of the Minister of Justice this afternoon, it might be thought that the present system is completely satisfactory; not only that the system is satisfactory but that in all cases the appointments made to the bench by the government have been entirely satisfactory. If the Minister of Justice would not pitch his case quite so high, it might not be necessary for the members of the house to take issue with him.
In all fairness, the present system is not entirely without merit. On the other hand the present system, and the appointments that have been made, in many cases have had obvious weaknesses. On the whole, we in Canada have a good bench. On the whole, it is the kind of bench of which this country can be proud. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, surely our aim in all these cases must be towards improvement and betterment at all times. I hope we are not going simply to be satisfied with the system that has been in vogue hitherto or the considerations that have determined judicial appointments hitherto. I think we should aim at a higher type of system, at a higher type of governing consideration, than has obtained in some of the appointments that have been made.
I wish to avoid generalizations in my remarks this afternoon, because the Minister of Justice has erred in indulging in too many generalizations.
The importance of a good bench, the importance of a bench that will command public respect, needs no comment. I should like to ask the minister, however, in the face of his admissions this afternoon that political 55704-1711
Supply-Justice
considerations are a factor in appointments that are made to the bench, if he can defend the system that is in vogue now as being a perfect system or a system that is better than any that could be devised. If he pays tribute to the intelligence of Canadians or to the intelligence of those who sit in the House of Commons, then I am going to challenge us all to apply that intelligence towards devising a better system and towards improving the whole judicial system.
The minister has rejected the reference to the English practice. I wish to make this observation about it, and I do not say it inany sententious mood. The minister was not slow to tell us in the house a week ago, with some degree of gratification, of the allowance by the judicial committee of the privy council of an appeal which was taken on his instructions from the Supreme Court of Canada to judges who were appointed under the English judicial system. Let us not be carried away by these appeals to local sentiment or when the minister talks in the way he has this afternoon, as though this were an issue of patriotism. I think, Mr. Chairman, that every man who cherishes an institution in this country as important to the whole fabric of our life as is our judiciary, should be satisfied with nothing less than the highest system of judicial appointments.
There are difficulties about comparing the English system of judicial appointments with the system in Canada. In this country we do not have an official who corresponds precisely to the Lord Chancellor, in whose hands the judicial appointments largely lie. Under our system the Minister of Justice exercises some of the functions of the Lord Chancellor as well as some of the functions of the Attorney General. He is a blend of the two functions, and so far as one can observe in this case, no matter how earnestly the minister exercises some of the functions that are exercised in Great Britain by the Lord Chancellor, nevertheless the functions that devolve upon him on the political side seem to many people to weigh unduly in the decisions that are made. I am not selecting the present Minister of Justice as a conspicuous example in that respect. I believe this debate has been on a very high plane. We are talking about a system under which the political functions discharged by the Minister of Justice, whoever he may be, in past administrations, the present administration or succeeding administrations, are very difficult to divorce from those other functions which are discharged under the British system by the Lord Chancellor.
Much of the criticism that exists today- and I hope the Minister of Justice is aware that there is a good deal of criticism of the

Supply-Justice
system-unquestionably arises out of the fact that we have had a long period of government under one particular party. It has gone on now for something like seventeen years. When you see appointments being made, with a few conspicuous exceptions, drawn from the one political party that is represented in the government for seventeen years, then you can see the accumulated errors of the present system. When governments change every six or eight years you do not find the accumulated effect of all the errors of the present system so evident as you do in a case where the government holds office for a longer period of years. If the political appointments, as under the present administration, are predominantly of the political stripe represented by the government, then you have exposed to public view and criticism the inherent errors and shortcomings of the present system.
I wish to say this in all fairness, because it seems to me that the Minister of Justice did not fully apprehend or fairly state the position taken by my colleague the hon. member for Kamloops. So far as I am concerned personally, I wish to make it quite clear that I do not consider an individual who has been in the service of the people of Canada in the House of Commons, or in any other elective office, is thereby disqualified for appointment to the bench. I cannot make my view too plain in that respect. That is one side of the position. On the other hand I think we wish to see, in the case of appointments that are made, much more taken into account than simply the fact that an individual has served, even capably, as an elected representative of the people either in parliament or in some other elective office. It is a question in every case of the merit and quality of the individual. Mr. Chairman, service in the House of Commons or any of the legislatures or in some other public office is no substitute for merit for appointment to the bench.
I should like now to say a word about defeated candidates. This matter was touched on last year, and the minister referred to the remarks that were made on that occasion by the hon. member for Macleod. The fact that a man has stood for public office should certainly be no disqualification when the government considers his merit for appointment to the bench. But the impression has gone abroad that, in many appointments made by the present administration, the fact a particular individual was a defeated candidate for public office or had stood for public office under the political banner of the Liberal party has been a dominant factor in the decision made by the government. These are subjects that have to be weighed with a

great deal of care. It seems to me that such a consideration as having supported the government of the day either in the House of Commons or in some other elected body, or having been a candidate for them at the polls, should not become the dominating consideration in making appointments. I suggest further that great care should be taken that there will be no suspicion or widespread feeling on the part of the public that these considerations have been predominant in the selection of men for appointment to the bench.
The Minister of Justice may defend what he has done, but he will not disabuse the minds of many of us in this committee or the minds of many people outside the chamber of the clear impression that these political considerations have, in many cases, largely decided appointments. The worst type of yielding to political consideration, it seems to me, is to be found in a situation which I think is fresh in the minds of many hon. members. There may be much to be said for the appointment of members of the house to the bench, if they are properly qualified; but it should not be made an occasion to put pressure on members of the house to yield anything of the independence that they ought to assert in the house. But what of a case where a member of the house resigns; where he is not appointed directly to the bench but, presumably knowing that he is going to be appointed, makes himself the campaign manager for the nominee of his party to succeed him at the by-election arising out of the vacancy created by his resignation? That is a situation which has arisen, Mr. Chairman; and I say that is the worst type of yielding to political considerations of which any government could be capable. Regardless of how popular or how well qualified the individual may have been, I say that the method followed in that case was inherently wrong; it cannot fail to bring the bench into that measure of disrespect and disrepute which is unthinkable in the minds of those who love and value democracy. Hon. members of the committee know quite well the case to which I refer. Such a thing should never be permitted to happen again.
It was in the minister's own province.

Yes. I wish to say one other thing, and I do this in the spirit of fairness. The minister has indicated that he has felt free, in times past, to consult the opinion of members of the house as to the fitness of those who were under consideration for appointment to the bench. I do not quarrel at all with that practice. I think there are many members of the house, particularly

those who are practising before the courts of their province, who are well qualified to advise the minister with respect to suggestions for appointment to the bench. However, in the minds of many in this committee and outside of it, I think there is more than a suspicion that the minister is either extremely selective in his choice of those whom he consults or that the area over which advice is sought is extremely narrow indeed. I say this in fairness to the minister: there is no reason that the minister should consult me. I am certainly not one of those who have ever been consulted. I do not know any member on this side of the chamber in the opposition who has ever been consulted. It would be interesting to know who they are, on what occasion, and the extent of the consultation of the Minister of Justice with them with regard to any appointment.
I said I did not intend to prolong this discussion. I think the discussion today has been on a high plane, and I hope it will have a useful effect. All I have said this afternoon has been said in the hope that it will contribute to correcting some of the impressions that might have been drawn from the minister's remarks this afternoon, where those remarks have erred seriously on the side of generalization and on the side of putting altogether too rosy a complexion on the considerations that enter into the selection made by the government of nominees to the bench.
The minister has ignored the fact that widespread criticism exists, and that the criticism is based upon more than suspicion. In view of the extent to which people who have been closely identified with the political life of his party have received judicial appointments, it is going to take more than the kind of statement the minister made this afternoon to answer the criticism that is being levelled from many sides today.

Mr. Chairman, I do not see why this discussion should be all left to the lawyers. I therefore should like to add just a word or two. I have long believed that in a democracy there is nothing in the world more important than to have the judiciary on the highest possible level. In these days when human relations have become so infinitely more complicated and when strange philosophies that we never even dreamed of now turn up even among those whom we thought were normal human beings like ourselves, I feel that the position of the judges is more than ever important. I therefore associate myself with all that has been said as to the importance not merely of appointing good men but, if possible, of doing it on a basis for which there shall be no means of criticism.
Supply-Justice
It is perfectly obvious that one of the things which will attract good men to the bench is the fact that the bench is on a high level. That is one of the reasons they get the best men in England; there the bench has a status, a dignity and a prestige which attracts men. The thing works both ways. It has that status, dignity and prestige because the best men come; and the best men come because it has that status, dignity and prestige. It seems to me that we should work to that end here.
In fairness I want to say that I think we have a great many good men on the bench. Like the hon. member for Eglinton, I believe the minister became a little bit enthusiastic this afternoon in some of the things he said. Nevertheless, the administration of the law would not stand where it does unless we had a lot of good men.
There is just one other thing I want to say. It is a kind of legacy from a member who sat in the last parliament and whom we all liked and respected. I refer to Mr. John Hackett. He made a point that I want to repeat, because one so often hears the opposite view taken. I repeat it because I think he was right. He protested again and again against the practice of detailing judges for all kinds of non-judicial functions. He pointed out that when judges get into things where human passions are involved, where there are strong economic differences among men, and into matters which are not primarily legal, inevitably they incur criticism in the minds of certain sections of the community, and that this criticism tends to drag them down from that position of impartiality and detached consideration of matters that come before them which I think is of great importance. Therefore, as a kind of proxy for Mr. Hackett, I raise that point again, as I consider it to be one of great importance.

Mr. Chairman, speaking in the interests of the layman, may I say there are one or two things that I think the minister should clear up. He has tried to assure us this afternoon that appointments to the bench are made on the basis of the individual's qualifications and ability, and that the appointee's political affiliation has not been a factor in the making of an appointment. It has been charged in the committee that during the sixteen or seventeen years the Liberal party has been in power, the appointments to the bench have been predominantly from Liberal supporters. Surely the minister can tell us just how many lawyers who were known supporters of other political parties have been appointed during those sixteen or seventeen years.

Supply-Justice
Surely there must be some good lawyers supporting other political parties, lawyers who have good qualifications for the bench. Inasmuch as in the last election fewer than 50 per cent of the voters in Canada were Liberals, I think we can assume that fewer than 50 per cent of the lawyers in Canada are Liberal. If that is a fair assumption, then one wonders how it is that there are not those in these other political parties who are qualified to fill these positions. That is the point I should like the minister to clear up for us. Name them.

He has not
given any names this afternoon.
Not very many.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No Conservative government could give you any names.

Before the item is carried I wish to refer to another matter, if the discussion on the subject of judicial appointments is concluded.
There is no provision in the Department of Justice Act at the present time requiring the department to make an annual report to the house. There are two annual reports which come to the house from the department. There is the one on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and there is the one that comes to us from the commissioner of penitentiaries; but unlike the statutory provision with respect to I think almost all the government departments, the Department of Justice Act, chapter 106 of the revised statutes of 1927, makes no provision whatever for an annual report to the house by the department. I think it would be helpful to the house, it would increase the knowledge of hon. members and would save the time of the house when we study the estimates of the department, if an annual report were rendered to the house by the department.
The department has today considerable areas of responsibility, governmental and legislative, which are not embraced within the scope of the two reports to which I have referred. They cover two important segments, it is true, but only two segments of the responsibilities of the department. I would urge that the Department of Justice Act be so amended as to require the rendering of an annual report by the department to the house. There are many good reasons for having such a report, and I can see no reason why there should not be one.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We would be glad to take my hon. friend's suggestion under consideration. In addition to the reports he named, there are other branches of the Department of Justice which make reports. Combines make a

report, and the bankruptcy division makes a report. Did my hon. friend mention the mounted police?
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are four reports instead of the two he has mentioned, and they cover a very large area of the department. But we can take under consideration the advisability of having a report concerning the residue of the department, which will be smaller than the area which is covered by these reports which I have named.

I rise to make no further reference or reply to the minister on the subject of judicial appointments, because I think a very useful and quite full debate has already taken place. I might just make this comment in passing. I was impressed by the readiness with which the minister, having dismissed for one purpose the tendency to look for examples of what goes on in England, refers to it gladly for another purpose when the example he quotes happens to conform to the argument he is at that moment advancing.
What I was going to ask the minister is with respect to the item, which I realize is small but nevertheless appears under this heading, of $3,000 for attendance at the judicial committee of the privy council. I observe it was not included last year, and I checked on last year's estimates and found that to be so, but it is included this year. I was not aware that there were any cases to be tried in the fiscal year now under review in which the government of Canada would have an interest. In any event it seems to me that, since the right of appeal to the privy council has been abolished, consideration should be given to amending or repealing that statute and taking that item from the estimates. Can the minister give us the position at the moment?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The position is that last year, notwithstanding the fact that the item was not included in the estimates, the chief justice did attend and did serve his time on the privy council. He went over this year, and the intention is that he should continue to go as long as there are appeals going from Canada to the privy council, but not after that.
The appeals will continue from Canada as long as there are cases which were current in some courts at the time the act abolishing the appeals was assented to in December, 1949. It is very difficult to forecast exactly when that will be, because it depends upon the rate of progress of the current cases through the courts. It may be some time before these current cases get to trial; and

alter the judgment is given, if there is any delay in the appeal to the first trial court and then to the supreme court, and so on, these delays may extend the time when such current cases reach the privy council, but when the last of them shall have been considered by the privy council, this item will disappear.

I should like to ask the minister a question. I do it now because there is no other place in the estimates I can do it. On many occasions the question was raised in the house of the minister taking under consideration the matter of enacting some legislation that would provide assistance for the lower income groups in the country who may become involved in lawsuits, to help them in carrying their cases to court. There has been a lot of discussion in the house. The minister remembers the discussions very well. That legislation exists in other countries. Because a large percentage of our people in the lower income groups cannot afford to go to the courts to get justice, some help should be given them. I thought we were making some progress there, because after a couple of discussions in the house I noticed that the bar association of Montreal had met and discussed the matter among themselves. They were going to set up some quasi-charitable institution among themselves to provide legal advice for those who were not in the position to pay for it. I notice that the bar associations of New Brunswick and Ontario have done the same thing. It looked to me then as if the legal profession were becoming alive to the necessity of this kind of thing. Perhaps they are a little bit afraid of legislation that would provide it by law.
I should like to know whether the department has been considering that matter and how far they have progressed towards some legislation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the Canadian constitution the exclusive authority over the administration of justice is vested with the provinces. I believe that in many of the provinces, as my hon. friend has rightly indicated, consideration has been given to this problem, which I think I am right in saying in most of them has taken the form of an offer made by the bar association or the law society to make available a list of volunteers including many of their best counsel to act for people who otherwise would not be able to afford legal help. That is true in my own province, and I think it is true in many of the others. They have done that in much the same way surgeons do in the hospitals. Oftentimes the man who has no money can get a much better surgeon than if he had just a moderate amount of money.
Supply-Justice
As a lawyer myself, perhaps I am a little prejudiced. I would think that sort of assistance would probably be more satisfactory and more effective than if it were provided by the provincial governments. But if it proved not to be so, then there would be nothing to prevent the provincial governments making assistance of that kind available if they wished to do so. Of course in certain cases for many years they have made it available. For example, if a man is charged with murder in the criminal courts the provincial government always sees to it that a counsel is appointed to defend him if he has not been able to instruct one himself.

I am not entirely satisfied with the minister's explanation. To begin with, this is not only a matter of administering the law. This is a matter of enabling a citizen who is not in a position to pay for legal services to obtain some assistance in the redress of a wrong. I know there are many warmhearted lawyers who will take such a case, provided it does not entail too much expense.
I am always suspicious of these voluntary organizations which spring up when some service of this kind is asked for. I think one of the main reasons we do not have a health program in this country is that every time we talk about it some new hospital scheme springs up to confuse us. I may be suspicious but I have noted that in two or three provinces some action was taken by lawyers when it was pointed out pretty strongly in the House of Commons that some assistance should be given.
I do not agree with the minister when he says it is the duty of the province only to administer the law. It is not a matter of administering the law, but rather one of enabling many citizens to take advantage of the law which exists. I do not ever expect that we will have this service on a provincial basis. I believe some serious study must be given to the matter by the federal Department of Justice so the provinces may have the benefit of guidance.
About a year ago I came in contact with a case in connection with which, I am sure, I had the same experience other hon. members have had. This was the case of a woman who had been struck by a motorcar and as a result spent nine months in hospital. She had a good case against an insurance company. For some time a lawyer was acting for her, but he did not make any progress. The only advice he gave her was to accept what the insurance company had offered-and that amounted to almost nothing. They said that they would pay the hospital bill and the nurses, but this woman had been crippled.

Supply-Justice
I talked to a lawyer who is a good friend of mine, and he pointed out that the woman had no money, and that if she wished to obtain any redress the case would have to be taken to court. The lawyer was not in a position to do that without having some money. I took hold of the case and succeeded in having it straightened out and obtaining what I considered was a reasonable settlement for the woman. But this was done through the threat of taking the matter to court. So far as I was concerned, it would have to go to court.
That is only one case. All of us come in contact with cases of that kind from time to time. I believe there should be a national law under which when a person is aggrieved and there is no doubt as to how the law would operate if the case could be taken to court, his interests would be looked after. I believe cases of that kind should be covered by a federal statute so that people on low incomes-even below the tax exemption- would have some assistance through a fund. I do not believe lawyers should have to work for nothing. They have their living expenses, and they have offices to maintain. My point is that some fund should be available out of which reasonable expenses could be paid to a lawyer when he has a case placed before him which, in his opinion, requires redress in a court of law, but where the aggrieved person does not have the money to go to court.
I would ask the minister to study the matter and at some time make a statement to the house as to what the cost might be and how it might be worked out. We are not infringing upon provincial rights or upon any laws now existing. It is the sort of matter that could be determined by the Department of Justice so that justice would be available to every citizen in Canada, regardless of financial status.

I should like to associate myself with what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I believe that through co-operation between federal and provincial authorities there could be at suitable centres men appointed who would act in a manner somewhat similar to pensions advocates. It would be the duty of such persons to see to it that people with cases to place before the courts might be able to do so, without being confronted with heavy expenses.

I have here a letter from
Chief Justice Rinfret, chairman of the statute revision commission, under date of May 23, 1952, only a few days ago. It is addressed to the Prime Minister, and reads as follows:
As chairman of the statute revision commission I feel that I should at this stage submit to you a report on the progress of the work.
We have reached a point now where all the material in both English and French versions has been consolidated, and, for the most part, set in type.
All the English material is set in type and has been revised by the commission in accordance with the authority conferred by the statute revision act. Final check proofs of the statutes in English are now being drawn and it is hoped that within a month or so all final copy for the English version will be in the hands of the printer.
The French version has also been completely consolidated and almost the entire French version is now set in type. The commission has engaged the translation bureau to revise the French version, and the bureau has now completed a little more than half the revision.
The statutes enacted at the current session of parliament cannot be included in the revision because we must now submit final copy to the printer. However, last year authority was obtained from parliament to issue a supplementary volume-
Members will recall that.
-and it is proposed to prepare, after the conclusion of the current session, a supplementary volume which will reflect the statutes passed at this session of parliament in terms of the new revised statutes so that when the new revised statutes are issued they will contain the complete and correct statute law as of that moment.
Early this year plans were made to have the revised statutes appear on the 1st January, 1953. We are, however, informed by the printer that at the current rate of progress, and having regard to the amount of other printing required, it will not be possible to bring the statutes out on that date and we should therefore contemplate the possibility that it may be some months after the 1st January, 1953, before the new statutes can appear. The printing task is, of course, an enormous one. Each version will run to nearly six thousand pages and in addition there will be tables, indexes and the proposed supplementary volume.
In addition, there will be tables, indexes and a proposed supplementary volume.
What is the date of that report?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May 23, 1952; just a few days ago.

I do not think any of us is likely to underestimate the immensity of the task, even from this point forward. One can only express the hope that if anything can possibly be done to bring the statutes into effect as of a convenient date such as the first day of a new year, it will be done.
My other question has reference to the honoraria paid to members of the Criminal Code revision commission. There is an item of $25,000 for this purpose. Will the minister indicate how that is to be distributed and what have been the honoraria paid to date? What will the total amount to by the time the task is completed?

speechtext: My information is that the amount that will be paid to those engaged will be roughly in proportion to the work they have done, with a ceiling of $7,500 to any one person for three years work.

speechtext:
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE ISO. Combines investigation branch, $261,055.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday
afternoon the minister indicated, in reply to a question from my colleague the hon. member for Kamloops, that at the present session legislation will be introduced for the purpose of amending the Combines Investigation Act; and indeed notice of a resolution to that effect has already appeared in Votes and Proceedings. I do not propose at this stage-indeed, it would be improper for me to do so-to embark upon an inquiry with regard to the scope or the extent of that proposed legislation. Nevertheless, it seems to me that at this point, where we are dealing with the estimates of the Department of Justice to provide for the combines investigation branch, this committee of supply will have to know something of the relationship between the estimate and the requirements of the proposed new organization of the combines investigation branch.
I can only assume that the legislation may follow at least to some extent, if not entirely, the recommendations made to the minister by the committee which was set up to study the combines legislation; I refer to the so-called MacQuarrie committee. As hon. members well know, this committee recommended a fundamental change in the structure of the combines investigation branch, featured by a separation of functions between the investigations and research agency on the one hand, and the board on the other. As the estimate before us, which is item No. 180, must have been drafted before there was any thought of introducing these far-reaching changes in the structure of the branch, I ask just what relationship this item of $261,055 is going to bear to the required expenditure of the new branch. I am wondering whether it might not be better to let this item stand over- and it is only a suggestion-until the house has considered the new legislation, in order that we may have some appreciation of the relationship between the new structure of the branch and the sum asked for by the government to sustain it.
