speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In connection with this matter I should like to make a few comments. The annual report of the commissioner of penitentiaries is a very interesting document which I strongly recommend to hon. members. However, it is a fairly thick volume, and I thought perhaps it might serve some purpose if I were to make a brief review of the more prominent highlights that might perhaps escape a perusal of the report itself, if it were of a rather hasty nature.
Has it been published?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, published and tabled. I strongly recommend that hon. members see it. It is a very interesting document indeed.
What is the date of this document?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951.
In September, 1947, the penitentiaries branch was reorganized with a view to implementation of the recommendations of the royal commission to investigate the penal system of Canada, better known as the Archambault report. During the intervening years an effort has been made to find practical means to interpret the rather general recommendations of the Archambault commission, in the light of the changed circumstances since the commission made its report.
Since the annual report of the commissioner of penitentiaries has recorded these developments in detail from year to year, it is not my purpose tonight to give a complete summary of everything that has taken place in the interval. It will suffice to say that we have gradually been replacing outworn and obsolete machinery and equipment in the penitentiary shops, that we have made every reasonable effort to improve personnel employed in the penitentiaries, and that major attention has been focused on the treatment of inmates to bring our practices more into conformity with recognized modem correctional procedure.
The basic purpose of the police forces, courts of law and penal institutions remains, as always, the protection of society. A temporary protection may be afforded by the removal of the offender from society and his incarceration for a longer or shorter period of time, as may be determined by the courts. Since, however, it is estimated that 98 per cent of all persons committed to institutions, no matter how long their sentences, will ultimately be released, it is important that during the period of imprisonment every effort should be made to change the basic habit

patterns and attitudes of the inmate so that upon release he may be better prepared to live a law-abiding life and to take his place as a fully functioning citizen.
Such a policy demands that all the resources and skills which may be made available in the handling of human beings should be applied in the day to day administration of the institutions. Considering the limitations imposed by the unnatural conditions under which persons live in penal institutions and the necessary concern for safety and security, this is not the easiest possible task. I believe, however, that during the past year we have made further progress in the development in our staffs of a better appreciation of the basic philosophy behind a truly correctional program. Though we are still faced with some problems of physical limitations by reason of inadequate or obsolete equipment, these difficulties are steadily being overcome; staffs of the institutions are now thoroughly aware of the objectives of the new program and are loyally supporting the efforts of the commissioner and his associates.
In June, 1951, a conference of all our wardens was convened in Ottawa. This was the second such conference that has been held in recent years. For a period of ten days the headquarters staff and the wardens of the penitentiaries discussed in detail problems of administration, and at that time far-reaching decisions were made regarding future developments. In the development of such a program as we have in mind it is essential that there should constantly be maintained an effective liaison between the headquarters staff which is charged with the responsibility for over-all administration and the institutional staff which has the day to day responsibility of translating general policy into daily procedures.
With the concurrence of treasury board a change in the remuneration rate for prisoners became effective on October 1, 1951. The old rate was 5 cents per day given uniformly to all prisoners whose conduct and industry was satisfactory. In effect this meant that as long as a man did not commit any acts of misconduct he received the daily remuneration, but this sum was inadequate to provide even a reasonable discharge allowance and did not make any distinction between inmates who were merely doing the minimum of daily work and those who were making better efforts. The new scale of remuneration, therefore, is a graded scale of 10, 15 and 20 cents per day, inmates being graded at intervals of three months not merely on their work efficiency but on their general conduct and

attitudes. A portion of the daily remuneration must be saved against the day of release; the balance may be spent for the purchase of small amenities such as chocolate bars, chewing gum, toilet supplies, etc. It is our hope that such a scale of graded remuneration will not only provide a somewhat more adequate discharge allowance but that it will also provide an incentive for better work in the penitentiary shops.
Consequent upon the introduction of increased remuneration, small canteens were established on December 1, 1951, through which inmates could make purchases of the comforts to which I have referred. In these canteens, however, no inmate is permitted to spend personal trust funds; he is only permitted to spend money which he actually earns in the institution. It was felt that any other policy would set up discrimination between inmates who had funds available and those who had none; it is an important principle of prison administration that no such policy of discrimination should be allowed to develop.
Another extremely interesting innovation of the past year was the authorization of inmate subscription to daily newspapers, without censorship. If it is hoped that prisoners will sooner or later return to the outside world, it is obviously necessary that they should not lose complete contact with what is going on in that outside world. In any case news sooner or later penetrates prison walls, and almost invariably in a perverted form. It seems to us much wiser to permit inmates to receive the news in the same way any other citizen may, and that he should also have the benefit of other material contained in the daily newspapers which will keep him in touch with the currents of thought and activity in the world to which he will return. This privilege has been much appreciated by the inmates and so far has presented no serious problems.
At Christmas of last year inmates for the first time were permitted to receive Christmas parcels from the outside. These were standard parcels of a value from $1 to $5, and arrangements were made by the individual wardens to have such parcels prepared by outside commercial suppliers provided the inmates themselves or their relatives made necessary funds available. The Christmas season in the institutions has in times past been a period of considerable emotional tension. The granting of this privilege in keeping with the sentiments of the season seemed to be a reasonable and humane act, and it was also much appreciated by the inmates. There were of course some inmates
Supply-Justice
who did not have funds available, but various arrangements were made that assured that no inmate would suffer because of lack of personal funds. It is only fair to the inmates to state that in many cases more fortunately placed inmates generously shared the contents of their parcels with their less fortunate fellows.
Since 1948 training courses for penitentiary staffs have been conducted in Ottawa, initially with the co-operation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and in accommodations provided by the police. It became obvious, however, that if such a training program were to be carried on effectively it was essential to have a permanent training centre devoted entirely to the training of penitentiary staffs. To achieve this end a suitable property already in the possession of the government was transferred to the penitentiary branch. The fine old residence has been entirely renovated by inmate labour, was furnished almost in its entirety with the products of penitentiary workshops, and on March 1 was opened as the penitentiary staff college.
Its location at Kingston is the logical one, inasmuch as it is in close proximity to Kingston and Collin's Bay penitentiaries and the prison for women, as well as having available the facilities of Queen's university with which it is hoped there may be increasing co-operation in our training program. Since March 1 two groups of guards from all institutions have attended, and there have been two conferences of senior officers. The establishment of this institution on a permanent basis is a recognition of the vital importance of continued training of penitentiary officers for their difficult and valuable work.
I previously announced plans for the development of a new institution in the province of Quebec in order to alleviate the overcrowded conditions at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary and to make better provision for the segregation of young and reformable types of offenders. Although not yet completed this institution, known as the federal training centre, contiguous to the penitentiary but under its own separate administration, has now reached the point where it can operate with its own staff and its own program. Suitable inmates, after a screening process, are transferred from St. Vincent de Paul to the new institution, and at the present time some 200 inmates have been so transferred. In this new institution an effort has been made to incorporate the best results of penal administrators elsewhere. Inasmuch

Supply-Justice
as all our penitentiaries are in a sense maximum security institutions, this too is a walled institution.
Emphasis, however, will be placed on education and vocational training. Considerable use already is being made of inmate committees in order to develop a sense of community responsibility. There is a greater measure of freedom allowed within the walls than is customary in most of our institutions. A mess hall has been provided so that inmates in this institution will eat their meals together. Further suitable facilities, hospitals, chapels, school buildings, etc., are now in the process of construction and will be completed in the not too distant future. The ultimate capacity of this institution will be 600 inmates.
There have been continued developments during the years in the recreational program, the hobbies program, in inmate publications and the development of inmate participation and responsibility through inmate committees operating under the direction of the staffs. Many of these developments have been fully reported in the daily press. It is interesting to note that in at least two areas penitentiary teams have been included in local city softball leagues and the standard of sportsmanship displayed in these contests has been a credit to the men in our institutions. Furthermore, such visits to the institutions have provided opportunities for certain members of the outside public to see something of the inside of prisons and to become familiar with a policy of administration which is humane and dedicated to the idea of rehabilitation.
Of course it would be ridiculous if all these efforts and others which are more fully described in the annual report, which as I said before I strongly recommend to hon. members, were not supplemented by efforts to assist the ex-prisoner to adjust himself at the time of his release. There have been continuing efforts in the organization of prisoners' aid societies, and such organizations are now functioning in practically every large community across the country. The national employment service through its special placements branch has been of invaluable assistance in this connection. The press also has presented fair, impartial and wholesome reports of our activities so that employers and the public generally have developed a much more sympathetic attitude to the problems of the ex-prisoner. The production by the national film board of two short ten-minute films, "Penitentiary" and "After Prison, What?", and the circulation of these films through the commercial theatres
[Mr. Garson.l
has also contributed in an effective way toward a better public understanding of the prison problem.
Prisons are inevitably places of considerable tension, but humane and scientific procedures can do much to relieve the tension. It has been effectively proven that a policy of repression or merely of punishment is really not reformative. Penal institutions must, of necessity, be disciplined institutions; but within the framework of good discipline and security it is possible to develop a "treatment" program which is not only scientifically valid but which is humane and Christian in its attitude towards the individual offender. Although we cannot claim as yet to have developed final and effective techniques in the treatment of the criminal, we feel that the policy which has been established, and which is being pressed forward aggressively, has resulted in a much improved institutional morale, and has had results even in a comparatively short time in the reduction of the percentage of penitentiary repeaters. It is our intention to continue the present program in the hope that a period of penitentiary imprisonment may not set a permanent stigma upon a man but that it may perchance provide, for all those who are amenable to treatment, a new view of life and living.
I should like to cite and pay tribute to some of the efforts that are being made to co-operate with us by public spirited organizations outside the prison walls. In December of last year the Rotary club of Kingston sponsored a four-day art exhibit of work done by inmates of Kingston and Collin's Bay penitentiaries and the prison for women. This exhibit was held in the auditorium of one of the Kingston hotels. It was opened at a regular meeting of the Rotary club which, according to reports, was the most largely attended meeting of the year. At a public meeting Professor Andre Bieler of Queen's university spoke on the place of art as a therapeutic device. The exhibit was open for four days and was largely attended by the general public. The entries were judged by Professor Bieler and prizes were awarded. A considerable number of paintings and drawings were sold, the proceeds going to the inmates' trust fund. This exhibit was an impressive demonstration of the talent which is available behind prison walls and, may I say, an impressive demonstration of the public spirit of the Rotary club of Kingston.
At Saskatchewan penitentiary on Saturday night, March 8, the associated commercial travellers sponsored an amateur hour over radio station CKBI, the whole program being

presented by inmates of the penitentiary. A suitable audience was gathered within the prison and the program relayed by telephone line to the broadcasting station. Donations were received over the telephone during the course of the evening and over $1,000 was realized for the work of the anti-tuberculosis league, one donation being wired from South Carolina and the balance coming from all over the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The inmates were naturally happy to be presenting a program over the air, and particularly pleased that they had been able to join in a worth-while community effort.
A final item which I would like to mention was the participation by a male chorus consisting of members of the Catholic and Protestant choirs of Dorchester penitentiary in the maritime music festival. The choir had been trained by the penitentiary organist, and their selections were transmitted by telephone line from the prison to the hall in Moncton where the contest was being held. The adjudicator awarded to the penitentiary choir the highest marks given to competitors in all classes. The program and the remarks of the adjudicator were relayed back to the prison and heard by all inmates over the prison public address system. A radio commentary on this program including a transcription of two numbers sung by the choir, "Drink to me only with thine eyes" and "O sacred head, once wounded" by Bach was heard over a trans-Canada network on Monday night, May 19.
I have mentioned these three events inasmuch as each of them in its own way was significant and unique. They are not isolated incidents but serve to illustrate the value of the recreational and educational programs which are now being introduced into our Canadian penitentiaries. Such programs provide a wholesome release for the tensions inherent in prison life. In some cases such programs have already proven their benefit in enabling released prisoners to gain acceptance in the community on their discharge; the notices regarding such events which have appeared in the public press and over the radio have served to provide for the general public a better understanding of a policy of "treatment" as opposed to the old philosophy of punitive deterrence.
I should like to conclude my remarks by quoting from an editorial which appeared in the Telegraph-Journal of Saint John, New Brunswick, dealing with the music festival and the part taken therein by the prison choir. It is headed "Prison choir in festival" and reads:
For a few days the newspapers were crammed with glaring headlines and frightening stories of prison riots, penitentiary fires and destruction of prison property.
Supply-Justice
It then goes on to list the places where this rioting has occurred. As we all know these details there is no purpose in reading them. The editorial then continues:
In some cases, hardened criminals held guards as hostages as they bargained for better food, liberalized parole systems and the dismissal of allegedly brutal officials. Throughout the land the voice of the convicts was heard. It was a hard voice, driving a hard bargain, and it was not pleasant to hear.
During this trouble it was natural to think of conditions in the maritime penitentiary at Dorchester and to wonder how the prisoners there were being treated. In view of this, it is rather interesting to note that the voice of the inmates of Dorchester will be heard publicly on Thursday night of this week. Only the prisoners of Dorchester will not be screaming out in riot, demanding more food and better conditions-at least, we do not anticipate anything of this nature.
What they will be doing is taking part in the music festival by singing "Drink to me only with thine eyes".
As a matter of fact, the voices heard will be those of twenty-four members of the prison choir which is to compete in the Moncton music festival. The enthusiastic members have been practising for the big night for the last six months. Of course, the prison choir will not be able to attend the music festival, so its selections will be piped direct from Dorchester into the Moncton high school auditorium. Arrangements also have been made for the adjudicator's remarks to be broadcast back to the choir over the prison's radio system.
The inmates, prison officials, the warden and the volunteer choir director all should feel proud of this achievement, which can be hailed as a new advance in prison recreation. It is the first time that a prison choir has competed in a music festival in Canada-and the voices which will be heard will be much more pleasant than the riotous cries which recently rang out-
It then goes on to name the prisons where trouble had occurred.
Is Bordeaux jail under federal or provincial jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is under provincial jurisdiction entirely.

Mr. Chairman, I think this statement by the minister is the best we have had in many years on prison reform. It indicates what is taking place in the prisons today. At other times when the minister's estimates have come up they have been passed before his officials were able to get down from the gallery and we were not given the opportunity to hear a statement of this kind. I think he has made up for it tonight.
I am delighted to know of the progress that is being made. A new commission was set up to do just these things, and I am sure that progress will continue to be made. I have a large penitentiary in my constituency and the welfare of the people, both inside and out, is of interest to me. I have studied the report to which the minister refers and I notice that the warden of that penitentiary

Supply-Justice
reports that far more non-fiction books were being read this year than ever before. It indicates that the training being given to the inmates is not being wasted. Then at page 89 of the report appears the following:
Our classification officer reports that the past year has been a year of marked progress, especially in our discharge program and excellent co-operation has been received from the national employment service, the prisoners' aid society, the Salvation Army, and other social agencies and it is gratifying to report good results on rehabilitation obtained.
These organizations deserve thanks for the work they are carrying on in helping prisoners get back into private life. I was wondering if the minister spent any time in the prisons when he was overseas.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not spend any time in the prisons, but I did pay a visit to the minister of justice of the then government of France. He was extremely interested in the work we were doing because our reputation had spread that far. He asked me to prepare a report upon what had been accomplished. I did that when I got back, but in the meantime the government had fallen.

The minister, being a good Manitoban like myself, I know would do nothing wrong that would get him into prison and I did not mean that. When I was over there a short time ago I was able through the kindness of the secretary for Scotland to visit some of the prisons. I was really astonished at how far they have gone in their work. I visited one prison at Peterhead in the north of Scotland, and I was told that they had not used the solitary confinement cell for seven years. Their treatment of prisoners is showing good results and I was surprised at the extent they have gone. They even have a bowling green and the inmates play golf and football. These men were allowed out to work on farms and brought back at night. They started to build the harbour fifty years ago, and it is not completed yet so there is still a lot of work ahead of them, but the farm work is more appealing than working on the harbour.
I visited the prison at Aberdeen, in which there is a different class of prisoner. The prisoners there find employment in making fish nets, and when I was there they were making fish nets to the accompaniment of radio music. I was assured by the governor of the prison that since this new system had been adopted the production of nets had increased by 50 per cent. I could go on for some time giving such details, because I spent quite a few days trying to find out things about the Borstal system and that sort of thing. They are doing a wonderful job. You have no idea how pleased I am to know that my own Canada is doing something
IMr. Bryce.]
along that line too, and I think we shall get good results. If these men could be reformed so they did not return to prison the taxpayers of the country would be saved a great deal of money spent in training custodians, wardens and that sort of thing.
I want to ask the minister about the 48-hour week. I asked him about it before, and he told me it is being considered. I had expected that by now a 44-hour week would be in vogue. Some problems had to be considered but I know some of the men are working 51 hours a week. Those are the men who go on duty at 7.30 in the morning and come off at 5.00 at night. The regulations state that if a custodian, or whatever you like to call him, works more than 3 hours overtime at any one time, then the department allows him for the overtime. These fellows only work a half hour per day overtime, which amounts to 3 hours per week, but they never get the 3 hours straight which would enable them to claim that time. I want the minister to know I fully realize that these men are on call in case of emergency, riot, fire or anything like that, so do not confuse the issue. I am considering the ordinary routine of the prison.
Then, too, the wages have been raised over the last four years but they have never kept pace with the wages paid to others. For instance, a man starting on the Winnipeg police force will receive $213.44 a month. This man who is a guard only receives $186 at the start. I think it is time wages were pushed up a little bit more to bring them at least close to the wages paid policemen. There is a difference now of $27.44 per month or $329.28 for twelve months. Possibly there should be a difference, but it should be not quite as great.
I should like to know also how many indeterminate prisoners there are. Has any consideration been given to doing away with corporal punishment? The other day I received a brief from the welfare council, and I was surprised to find that this form of punishment has been eliminated in every civilized country in the world except Canada and certain of the states in the United States. This brief was forwarded by the Canadian welfare council, 245 Cooper Street, Ottawa, and it is over the signature of R. E. T. Davis, executive director. Will the minister state what consideration has been given to eliminating corporal punishment in this country?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Dealing with the hon. member's questions in order, I wonder if I could begin by having him clear up a point for me. Does the member of the Winnipeg police force of whom he spoke receive any living accommodation in addition to his salary?
The wardens at Stony Mountain pay their rent, too.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The information I have is that the guards who come on the force at Stony Mountain-I presume that is the penitentiary the hon. member is interested in-start at $202 per month. If they are single men and living in, they get their living accommodation as well. I believe, therefore, that the two wage rates compare quite favourably.
Now with regard to the indeterminate sentences, there are 25 such prisoners in the entire penitentiary system, that is including all the penitentiaries in Canada.
With regard to the matter of corporal punishment, that is a matter which is covered by the Criminal Code, the revision of which should be back from the Senate one of these days and my hon. friend can speak to this section at that time.

I should like to make one or two observations about what the minister said in connection with the maritime penitentiary, and the choir which took part in the music festival. This festival was sponsored by radio station CKCW, Moncton. The Prime Minister opened that festival, and he paid fitting tribute to the members of the choir. As the minister has said, this choir made the highest marks of any entered. It is interesting to note that one of the members of the choir had been discharged from the penitentiary, and in order to take part in the competition he returned to the penitentiary at his own expense. I believe the warden and his staff are to be congratulated on making these facilities available to the choir.
There is one other point that has not been mentioned very often, and that is the rehabilitation of these men when they are discharged. The John Howard society and the unemployment insurance commission are doing an excellent job, and they are to be congratulated. The work must be effective, because the population of the penitentiary is gradually decreasing.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask three or four questions. First of all I should like to make one or two general observations. Though we all sympathize fully with the aims of the penitentiary administration, particularly since we received the recommendations of the Archambault report, I think we all feel that the old idea that it was nothing but punishment and protecting society by shutting up people behind walls has now gone, and we recognize that what we are trying to do is not only protect society but turn the offenders into better citizens. At the same time, I think we must not get to the stage where we talk about it as if being there was a reward for meritorious
Supply-Justice
service. I am sometimes just a little bit afraid that we are getting sentimental about it. For example, I am all in favour of education and proper recreation-
Training.

Yes, training; but when I hear of teams from the penal institutions taking part in city leagues, I am just a little bit troubled by this thought. I am not thinking so much about the inmates themselves; I am thinking about the people who play with them. Are we making this into something which is trivial? Are we in danger of sentimentalizing about i-t? I should like to hear what the minister has to say about that matter. I think it is a great pity if we are getting sentimental about this thing. After all, it is not a sentimental matter. It is a serious matter. We all agree that we must behave in a humane manner and must do our best to retrain these people. On the other hand, as I say, I think we should keep the thought clear in our minds that this is a serious matter and that these men are there because of the things they have done against society.
May I now ask one or two questions. From the report I am not clear to what extent young offenders are segregated. Will the minister say a word about that matter?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To reply to my hon. friend's question, the answer is that in the large institutions-for example, at St. Vincent de Paul-we have the federal training centre that I was referring to just tonight, which has been built for the express purpose of segregating youthful offenders and also those who seem to offer better hope of rehabilitation than do others. That is also true of Kingston and Collin's Bay. With regard to the other penitentiaries, we segregate the living quarters of the juvenile offenders and maintain that segregation in all other respects as far as our physical facilities permit us to do so. But the limitation there is simply that of our physical facilities.

I should like to ask further whether the objection to young offenders being with the old lags is not so strong that segregation ought to be a matter of top priority, almost ahead of everything, in order to keep the young people by themselves. I should like to have the department's opinion on that matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I cannot emphasize too strongly that the principle of segregation is strictly followed in their living quarters; and that is where they spend a great deal of their time.

Supply-Justice
Is that segregation of living quarters followed everywhere?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. As I said before, where we have large institutions like St. Vincent de Paul and its associate federal training centre, and Kingston penitentiary and its associate, Collin's Bay, there is complete segregation; because the one institution in each case is just for the one class of offenders. In the other institutions we carry out the policy of segregation to the fullest extent which is possible, having regard to our physical facilities. In all cases we provide for segregation of living quarters.
And of work?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; not of work.

Does the
minister not think that segregation is the most important of all?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not entirely. The commissioner tells me that some of the young offenders are pretty hard characters. He says that in some cases they are just as hard as the old ones.
With regard to the suggestion by my hon. friend to the effect that we are going sentimental, if he will permit me to do so I must repudiate it. I do not think we are going sentimental. We have not at any point gone beyond the stage where we can justify this thing in terms of dollars and cents if not on any other basis; because as my hon. friend knows, when crime and the incidence of crime is not on the decline, the rate of recidivism in our Canadian penitentiaries in the last five years has declined from 45 per cent in 1947 to 40 per cent in 1952.
In that connection, will the minister turn to paragraph 31 on recidivism, because I do not understand some of the figures. Will the minister per cent in 1947 to 40 per cent in 1952.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These figures I have just quoted are the rates of recidivism for the penitentiaries. These are not the rates applicable to any of the provincial jails. I maintain that in a matter of this kind-and I think my hon. friend will agree-the proof of the pudding is in the eating. If at a time when crime is not on the decline and society tends to produce more crime and more criminals we can reduce the rate of recidivism quite substantially over a period of five years in our penitentiaries, I think that fact shows that we are not pampering them very much. We are producing a good result.

I want to correct one impression that I did not intend to give the minister. I was not accusing the

department of being sentimental. I was saying I was a little bit afraid that there might be sentimentality in certain quarters. I was merely asking the question prompted by the incident to which he referred. Will the minister explain for me paragraph 31 at page 12? First of all it says:
The general percentage of recidivism-all types of sentences-is 76-3 (previous year, 77-1).
Then it goes on and gives certain details. Then it gives the percentage of penitentiary recidivism as 38-71. Does that top figure of 76-3, which struck me as an alarming one, apply to all types?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.
That seems to be a large figure. Is there any explanation for it? If you have three quarters or over who are repeaters, it seems rather disappointing.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite true. But the figure I am speaking about is the figure which is a measure of the effectiveness and efficiency of the penal institutions. We cannot take any responsibility at all for any of the other institutions.

If I may, I should like to ask just one other question. Will the minister say something more about education? I take it that education is limited as to hours, because I presume the men have their fixed hours of work. I should like to know what hours are available for education, and I should like to have some significant figures showing to what extent it is availed of. I should like to know what tests the department have. I have no doubt they have very significant tests which they can give to us so we may have an idea as to what is really being done here.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think perhaps the best way I could iput it for my hon. friend would be to refer him to the section in the report which outlines in considerable detail what the educational facilities are. If he will turn to page 15 he will see, commencing there and going on for several pages, to the top of page 18, a full statement on the educational facilities at the penitentiaries.

Mr. Chairman, I think one thing this discussion this evening has brought out is the fact that here we have a report that deserves much more study and much closer examination than we are able to give it in a committee of the house such as the one we have at the present time. I would suggest to the minister that some thought be given to presenting this annual report to a special committee before which officials of the minister's department can be invited

as witnesses and who can answer from firsthand knowledge just such questions as those which the hon. member for Greenwood has been raising tonight. There is a value in giving members of the house a greater opportunity than a committee of the whole affords to learn more of what is being done by the officials of the minister's department in connection with our penitentiaries. I notice on page 8 of the report, for instance, that during the past year increasing efforts have been made to gain the interest and co-operation of the general public in the activities within the institution. My suggestion is that in order to gain the interest and co-operation of members of the house in the activities that are going on within these institutions a report such as this be presented to a special committee of the house.
I want to congratulate the officials on the presentation of this report. There is certainly plenty of evidence that the minister has in his department men and women of imagination and intelligence, and with a good deal of sympathy for the people with whom they are dealing. What I am particularly delighted with is the section of the report dealing with educational activities within these institutions. I think one of the most remarkable bits of information is that part of the report which states that since 1947 only 15 per cent of those who have graduated with vocational training courses have got into trouble with the authorities after their release, and that 95 [DOT] 6 per cent of those who graduated during the year with which this report deals became non-repeaters. That I think is a remarkable record, and one for which the minister and his officials are to be complimented.
Incidentally, I might remark that another reason for sending this report to a committee would be to get more up-to-date information. Nothing in this report pertains to anything that has taken place within these institutions since March, 1951, fourteen months ago. I note in one place, for instance, that at the time this report was written plans were being drawn for a new building at Kingston penitentiary. The report said it was hoped that construction would commence on this project during the summer of 1951. I would like to know just what progress has been made on that building. The minister might give us that information.
I would like to know to what extent the educational work within these institutions is hampered by lack of facilities, equipment and accommodation. I can understand that officials of the department are very hesitant about including such information as that in the report. If we could get some of these officials before a committee of the house we
Supply-Justice
could find out just how much more we in this parliament could do to promote the good work of those who are carrying on within the institutions.
Can the minister tell us briefly just what new facilities, equipment and buildings have been made available for those who were attempting to carry on educational work in those institutions during the past year.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Since that report?
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say to begin with that the building to which my hon. friend referred as having been mentioned in that report is now under construction, but it is not completed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the minister two or three questions. First of all I wonder whether the federal training centre associated with St. Vincent de Paul and any other similar institutions have been in operation long enough for him to give us the rate of recidivism in connection with them as compared with the rate generally.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well the federal training centre at St. Vincent de Paul opened only in April, 1952, so it obviously has no statistics. The senior assistant commissioner tells me that at Collin's Bay over a period of 15 years, from 1930 to 1945, he has made a calculation of the rate of recidivism, that is of those who having been discharged from Collin's Bay, have gone out and got into trouble and come back into the penitentiary system. That would not include those who may have got into trouble and got into a provincial jail- that would not turn up in our statistics-the figure for that, as compared with the 40 per cent and 45 per cent I was mentioning a moment ago, was 20 per cent. That is the graduates, if you like, of Collin's Bay and the like came back to the penitentiary system to the extent of 20 per cent over a period of 15 years, from 1930 to 1945.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question or two with respect to the St. Vincent de Paul training centre. He said there were about 200 young men there now; that the accommodation when the institution is completed will be around 600. Will the other 400 be transferred from that same penitentiary, or will they be transferred from other parts of Canada? The same type of question could apply to Collin's Bay.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The information I have at the present time is that we have accommodation for 400 people, and of that total accommodation one building accommodating 100 people is set aside temporarily for administration. Therefore this leaves us with a net accommodation of 300 which is available at the moment. In that accommodation for 300 we

Supply-Justice
have segregated, as they came from St. Vincent de Paul, suitable convicts for that type of training provided there. We will continue that policy until we have the 300 filled. By that time we hope we will have the space for the 600 completed and available, and we then can consider transferring prisoners from other institutions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is there any similar accommodation or institution for prisoners in other parts of Canada? For example, I understand there is no such institution as a federal training centre associated with Stony Mountain. Meantime prisoners from there are not being transferred, although they might be in the same category. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I said in reply to a question asked earlier by the hon. member for Greenwood, we bring our program forward as we are able to make the physical facilities available to carry it into effect. We cannot go faster than that. We can transfer from other penal institutions these special types of prisoners only up to the limits of the accommodation we have for them.

I listened with interest to what was said by the Minister of Justice. I was surprised that so much stress should be laid on these improvements in connection with penitentiaries, because I thought all these things had been put into effect long ago. The Archambault report came out in 1947, five years ago. That seems to me a long time to elapse before recommendations receive consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Have you read the 1919 platform of the Liberal party?

Would the minister look at page 52 of the report to which he referred, which gives the previous convictions in respect of eight penitentiaries. With respect to Newfoundland he will find that out of 30 inmates there were 18 with no previous convictions. I believe that is the highest proportion shown. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to St. Vincent de Paul. This table shows that at that penitentiary there were 72-7 per cent recidivists, while in Newfoundland it is only 40 per cent.
In Newfoundland we have only one penitentiary, and I do not believe it could be so described, to use the strict sense of the word, because it also takes care of those people who are sent from the magistrate's court in St. John's. How does the minister manage to keep the penitentiary records segregated, and what proportion of penitentiary costs are borne by the federal government, and what proportion by the provincial government?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In Newfoundland the federal government pays the provincial government for all the prisoners in the jail there who are sentenced for more than two years or who, in other words, would otherwise be eligible for incarceration in a penitentiary. We pay Newfoundland on a per diem per prisoner basis.
At one time there was a prison logging camp. Is that still being operated under the federal government?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a provincial government operation.

I should like to ask a question concerning a problem of great importance, one that is broader than just the aspect pertaining to penitentiaries administration. I refer to the problem of the treatment of sex offenders. What progress is being made in this field? I am aware of the report submitted to the minister's department over a year ago by the John Howard society of Ontario, which dealt with legal and psychiatric aspects of the problem and was accompanied by proposed legislative enactments. Would the minister give us a report on this subject, please?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I am thinking of the same report the hon. member has in mind, the one which came out about a year ago, my recollection is that it was more or less factual, and did not contain any recommendations for treatment. It just reviewed the facts. Speaking also from memory I believe we made provision in the law two years ago

and the hon. member will recall this-whereby courts could impose a special type of indeterminate sentence in respect of sexual offenders. The last time I had occasion to check it up it seemed to me that very small use was being made of that legislation. Of course it is a straight question of the administration of law and the exercise of discretion by the courts.

Has consideration been given to the amendment made at that time? I remember offering some criticism of the amendment in the house, and further amendments were introduced as the legislation passed through committee of the whole on that occasion. Is that legislation under review now to determine its effectiveness, or to what extent further progress can be made, either by legislative or other means?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the normal course of events I think this matter came under the consideration of the commission dealing with the consolidation and revision of the new Criminal Code. The Criminal Code bill will return to

this chamber in due course from the Senate, and can be considered at that time.

Could not the minister be a little more informative in a general way as to how the department plans to deal with this problem? This is a serious matter which has been considered by the house on one or two previous occasions. It is causing a great deal of concern not only here but throughout the country. I think the committee ought to have an informative statement as to what the government is doing to meet this problem.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will agree that the problem divides itself in this way. First of all there is the enactment of the necessary criminal laws to deal with offenders of that kind. This would be part of the criminal law, and its enactment is the responsibility of this parliament. Then the administration of such criminal law is a matter for crown attorneys appointed by the provinces or municipalities. The adjudication of the offences charged is carried out by courts appointed by the provinces. If the courts have invoked the provisions we have made in the law especially for these sexual offenders, the offenders go back in some cases to provincial prisons and in other cases to penitentiaries, with indeterminate sentences. When they come to us-and that is what we are now discussing-we are more fortunate than the average provincial prison because we have a psychiatrist in our service who can give consideration to these offenders and give as good therapeutic treatment as can be devised for their cure. I think it might be possible for greater use to be made of these indeterminate sentences for sexual offenders. But that is a matter of administration of the law, and not of any defect in the law itself.

I have a few words to say on this item. Unfortunately I have not been able to go through the entire report, but perhaps members will be pleased because for that reason my remarks will therefore be shorter. For a number of years I have been following the policy with respect to penitentiaries, and I wish to add a word of commendation for the implementation, so far as it has gone, of the Archambault report. I think great progress has been made along two lines, general care of and attention to inmates of the institutions, and particularly the training program for the guards. That has been a most useful program indeed, and possibly has done more than anything else to make the administration of the penitentiaries more efficient than was the case in the past.
I am interested in one particular problem, and perhaps the minister can give me some
* Supply-Justice
information along this line. I note with interest the educational program within the institutions. I think that is very much to the good, but for the last four or five years now I have wanted to secure information as to the educational qualifications of the inmates on admission. I do not see that this information is available in the report, and I hope it can be made available in the future. There are one or two sections of the report dealing with education to which I should like to draw attention. On page 15 of the report, paragraph 48 reads as follows:
Classes for illiterates and low literates continue in all penitentiaries on the same basis as they have been conducted for many years.
What strikes me as odd about that is that although there are only eight institutions with 4,817 inmates, yet in each institution there are obviously illiterates and low literates, and I think they are out of proportion when compared with illiterates and low literates in the rest of the population. Then I note that on page 18 it mentions the fact that the schoolteacher at Kingston penitentiary made a survey of the educational qualifications of the inmates there, and his findings are as follows:
per cent
Illiterates	 3-7
Grade 7 or less	approximately 35 0
Grade 8, but not a full year at high school 30-0
Some high school	 25-0
Completed high school	 4-0
One or more years at	university	 1*7
Then our attention is drawn on page 24 to a survey at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and paragraph 8 on that page reads as follows:
Seven hundred and fifty cases were studied with regard to educational standing. Sixty-one per cent were reported as VI grade or below, 34 per cent from grades VI to IX and 5 per cent tenth grade or higher. These figures are on the basis of inmates' own reports and may therefore perhaps indicate academic achievement somewhat higher than is actually the case.
My point is that I think we should have the educational qualifications of the inmates in these institutions made available to us. I have not the facts but I think the standard of education of the inmates is below that for the country as a whole. I believe there is a distinct correlation between crime and lack of education. Consequently I would be pleased if the minister could give us any more information on that point than I have been able to discover, or his assurance that for the future information along that line will be compiled. After all, these men in the penitentiaries are costing us more than any other individuals in Canada. It has always seemed to me that it would be wiser to spend more money on education and eliminate the

Supply-Justice
illiterates rather than keep them in penitentiaries for years at heavy expense and then try to educate them.
I feel that the follow-up program after men leave the penitentiaries is good as far as it goes, and I think a great deal of credit is due to those people who, through various societies, have interested themselves in men who are released from penitentiaries, who find them employment and assist them to become members of society again. I have talked to people who have been doing that work for years, and they have pointed out to me the extreme difficulties involved in some instances in getting men settled in society again, although sometimes it is not too difficult. My feeling is that in some way greater responsibility should be accepted by the department for completing the rehabilitation of the men who are released. After all we have a very fine program now within the institutions which prepares them for their return to society. After they have served their terms and paid their debt to society they should be accepted again in so far as it is possible. With a proper program of returning men to their positions in society we might have fewer men returning to the penitentiaries.
I think it is at this point that our program is perhaps somewhat weak. If the department could see its way clear to institute a follow-up program that would look after these men more adequately from the time of their release from penitentiary and for such period as is necessary afterwards, it would be advantageous. On page 29 of the report I notice that paragraph 115 deals with the after care of prisoners and reads as follows:
Following the policy established initially in 194849 federal grants-in-aid have been made available to recognized prisoners' aid organizations, rendering effective service to prison dischargees. A total of some $27,250 was expended for this purpose.
I wonder if that amount of money has been adequate to meet the need. If more assistance were provided at that point we might save at the other end. Instead of having to pay out the taxpayers' money to maintain recidivists in our penitentiaries, would it not be better to spend a little more at an earlier stage and make sure they did not return?
How many of the penitentiaries are on a five and a half day week?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All of them.
We have had quite an ample discussion, but I think we should have some comment or reply from the minister in connection with the well-considered remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: 1 certainly would not want to overlook my hon. friend who was a colleague of mine in the Manitoba house for some time, but I did not understand that he wished me to reply. These prisoners' aid societies operate on the basis of grants which they receive from us and also from the provinces because they also place prisoners discharged from the provincial jails. Being charitable organizations they have endowments and the like of their own. My hon. friend has suggested that we might ourselves deal with all discharged prisoners but I am told, and this *can be readily understood, that in many cases prisoners prefer to deal with a voluntary agency.
I was not expecting the department to deal with them; I was suggesting that the department be more generous in the assistance given to the voluntary agencies.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I may say that we have been satisfying the requests of these agencies. My hon. friend has had some experience in that field and he will know that agencies of this sort usually are not too reticent about making requests. This amount has been increasing as time went on and I have no doubt that if the volume of work increases the grants may be increased accordingly.
Could the minister say something with regard to the educational statistics I was asking about?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's suggestion is good. As far as I am concerned I shall be glad to discuss it with the officials to see whether it is feasible to introduce it.

Do the voluntary agencies take in hand everyone discharged from the institutions, or do they just do their best? Do they assume the responsibility of trying to assist everyone who comes out and is in neeed of assistance?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The voluntary agencies, the Salvation Army and the national employment service provide service for all discharged prisoners who wish it. We do not compel prisoners to receive such services but it is known to all prisoners that this service is available. I might point out that when a man comes into a penitentiary he is interviewed by a classification officer and his strong and weak points as well as his background and so on are carefully analysed. This personnel officer and the chaplain as well as the psychiatrist, if necessary, are in touch with the prisoner during his period of incarceration.
Some time before his discharge he goes, if he wishes, not only before the classification

officer but before a representative of the voluntary agency; and the problems he is likely to face when discharged are discussed with him. The classification officer maintains contact at all times with the voluntary agencies and the employment office. Thus if the prisoner has any interest at all in getting re-established he is strongly encouraged before leaving the penitentiary to go to these outside agencies, and in a great many cases he does go. In the report of the Massey commission attention is called to the fact that Canada has no adequate botanical gardens. It goes on to say that in this deficiency Canada is unique among the advanced countries of the world. I have a list prepared which sets out where some of the principal botanical gardens are located, and which supports this statement of the Massey commission. The first one on record is at Pisa in Italy, which was established in 1534. That was followed quickly by others in Oxford, England, in 1621; Chelsea, in 1673; Paris, France, in- 1635, and so on. The result is that practically all the principal countries of the world have botanical gardens. The Massey report goes on to say at page 325:
A general collection or collections of all types of plants is needed not only for the pleasure and instruction of citizens but for scientific purposes.
Then it goes on to say that from the economic point of view it is not likely there could be one botanical garden established in Canada which would serve all purposes, because of our varying climatic conditions. Actually there is a small botanical garden at the present time in Montreal, and there is what is known as the royal botanical garden in Hamilton. I know the historical society of Victoria made certain definite recommendations to the Massey commission suggesting that a most suitable place west of the Rocky mountains would be the southern end of Vancouver island, where we have climatic conditions which are unequalled the world over for the growing of a large variety of flowers, bushes and trees.
Not only from the point of view of pleasure but from the point of view of the development and application of the science dealing with shrubs and plants to the industries of Canada, the government would certainly be warranted in following the recommendation made by the Massey commission and establishing these botanical gardens as soon as possible. Has any consideration been given either to the establishment of one central botanical garden, which is not recommended in this report, or to granting assistance to existing or projected botanical gardens throughout Canada? I should like to inform the minister that consideration is being given by a number of horticulturists on the southern portion of Vancouver island to the establishment there of a botanical garden. They hope the government and the minister will see their way clear

to assist in the establishment of that garden. Can the minister say whether any progress has been made along these lines?

Therefore if the government follows the report of the Massey commission this will be something to be dealt with by the Minister of Agriculture. The Prime Minister indicated yesterday that step by step the government does intend to implement the various recommendations of the Massey commission. I can only say to the committee now that I am very glad to have these views expressed by the hon. member, and I assure him that they will be borne in mind.

If and when the government do consider the support of botanical gardens, I would urge them not to overlook the royal botanical gardens which have been established in the Hamilton area in connection with McMaster university. I would also suggest that I do not think the Department of Agriculture is the one to deal with this very important matter.

I should like to add a word to what the hon. member for Wentworth has said because this is a matter with which I have had considerable experience, inasmuch as it comes under the jurisdiction of the parks board of the city of Hamilton. This particular botanical garden is not only a plant life but also a wildlife preserve. Not only does it provide for the production and development of various types of animal and plant life but, as the hon. member for Wentworth has said, it has been the means by which McMaster university has carried on much of its scientific research in these fields. I know that the work of the garden has been seriously hampered for many years through lack of funds. There are two matters under this item that interest me. The first has to do with the disappearance of an item from the estimates this year. I spoke on this matter on March 17 last, so the facts are before

Supply-Resources and Development members of the house. I refer to the grant of $15,000 that was made available to the international peace garden on the Manitoba-North Dakota boundary. My reason for raising this inquiry tonight is to see if I can discover the present status of the international peace garden. I think the minister is well aware of the facts. Various representations have been made, and they are endeavouring to cope with the emergency that has resulted from the withdrawal of support for the current year.
As I pointed out on March 17 the garden, which has been under way since 1932, had reached a crucial point in its development. In a matter of two or three years it would have been completed successfully provided this support had been maintained. I further pointed out that it had great potentialities, and as a matter of fact it has already demonstrated that it is a significant tourist attraction. There is a paved road now through the garden and a new customs building is to be established. The money is provided in the estimates for the current year. With the completion of the highway and the enlargement of the customs facilities tourist traffic is going to increase tremendously because of the significance of the international peace garden. It is beginning to be recognized as an international shrine and has tremendous appeal to United States tourists. I know there are other hon. members who are interested in the fate of the peace garden grant and who have made representations along these lines. That is the first item I wish to bring to the minister's attention.
The second point is the increase in the schedule of camping fees in the national parks. This increase has been right across the board. As a result of a question I asked I have discovered that in most cases the increase in camping fees has been 100 per cent. I should like to know whether this increase is due to greater costs and the prevailing high prices, and whether the parks were able to pay their way under the old schedule. In other words I am wondering whether it was financially necessary to increase these national parks camping fees.
As I understand it, the national parks were established originally in the early thirties and designated as the people's playgrounds. There is a feeling that the parks are being commercialized, and this has been dealt with editorially by such famous columnists as Jack Scott. As an example, some of the citizens of Brandon who use the facilities of the Manitoba national park at Clear lake have been in the habit of establishing their tent houses in the tourist camp in May in order to hold the site. They pay the weekly rental

through the entire season to the end of September, which represents an investment of some $40. This is considerably higher than the taxes paid by the more prosperous citizens who are able to build cottages in the park. I should like to know whether this increase has been necessitated by losses in the operation of the parks or whether it is an attempt to supplement income for improvements and so forth.
I understand a charge of $1 is made for commercial vehicles travelling through the parks and I should like to know whether that requirement could be met on the basis of an annual licence.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the St. Lawrence national park. The hon. member for Brandon referred to the international peace garden, and I should like to mention that for many years there has been a movement in Ontario, the county of Leeds especially and at the section crossed by the Thousand islands bridge, to establish a national peace park. At times this movement has had considerable impetus; at other times it seems to drag, and we do not hear much about it.
As the committee are probably aware, the Thousand islands bridge was opened in August, 1938. It crosses one of the most beautiful sections of the Thousand islands in the St. Lawrence river. The Canadian span has piers in no less than two of the St. Lawrence national parks. As the bridge ends on Hill island it crosses a road about three-quarters of a mile long to the Canadian customs. There is then one of the shortest international bridges in the world, a bridge less than sixty feet in length which crosses the international border. The route then passes on to beautiful Wellesley island in the state of New York. The bridge was opened by the late President Franklin Delano Roosevelt and our late Prime Minister, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. On that historical occasion Mr. Roosevelt made his famous statement about the waters of the St. Lawrence. He said that while these had always divided the two countries he hoped that in the near future they would serve as a closer bond between the two countries. He was referring to the St. Lawrence seaway and power development.
Not only is this Thousand islands section of the St. Lawrence river one of the most beautiful on the continent, it is very important historically. I for one would hate to see that splendid idea of creating an international peace park at this place dropped. My purpose in rising tonight is to remind the minister and the committee that this is a project which is too important to be forgotten. It

concerns sections of Canada and the United States which have great historical interest.
I understand that at one time our national parks branch had prepared elaborate and beautiful plans for this park. I understand also that at one time the state of New York was co-operating closely in the project. Then the war came along and the plans were forgotten. They were revived again after the war, but of late little has been heard of this scheme on either side of the border. I might say that originally the plans called for an international golf course, nine holes to be in Canada and nine holes in the United States, with two water holes where you would drive back and forth across the international boundary, or you would if you were lucky. This matter is of such importance that I want to bring it before the committee for the consideration of the minister and to have it on the records that this great project be not forgotten.
It has been my custom in recent years to mention our St. Lawrence national parks and what they have meant to the people, and at the same time to urge the department to set up similar parks along the Rideau river. These are not large parks like Jasper or Cape Breton island; they are small parks which can be enjoyed by the general public. They have pavilions, bathing facilities, docks and stoves, and I know of no other place where the public enjoy themselves more.
I have felt for years that parks similar to the popular ones on the St. Lawrence should be established in the Rideau district. If the hon. member for Lanark were here I know he would support me, because I have spoken to him about it. Part of the Rideau lakes are in his riding, part in my riding and part in the riding of the hon. member for Frontenac. Actually there are natural facilities, the property of the dominion government, which could be easily converted into national parks similar to those on the St. Lawrence. There are various places in the county of Leeds, although actually they are used more by the people of Lanark, that could be made into national parks. There are other equally admirable sites which could be magnificent parks at Rideau Ferry, another one at The Narrows; another one at Foster Lock; another one at Chaffey's Locks, and so on all the way from Smiths Falls to Kingston. I urge the minister that a survey be made with the idea of establishing these parks along this great and beautiful waterway which connects the capital of Canada with the city of Kingston.
This section of the country is also of great historical importance, but most important of all it would appear to be an ideal spot to which to bring families to enjoy to the utmost 55704-173
Supply-Resources and Development the magnificent scenery which is found in that part of the province. It would be a great boon to the people living in the city of Ottawa. I understand there are excursions which run from Ottawa to the Rideau lakes by bus, and from Smiths Falls through part of the waterway by motorboat. If it were possible to have these national parks established around the right of way, it would make another section of Canada that would afford great pleasure to the public. Not only would the people from this immediate district go there, but also people from eastern Ontario and part of the province of Quebec. I go further and say that it would be a great attraction to tourists from the United States.

Mr. Chairman, the Rideau has been mentioned so I think the Trent should be mentioned also. In the Trent system we have 250 miles of lakes and rivers. There are many beautiful spots along the Trent where government lands have, in some cases, been beautified by the people of the area so the public can enjoy the scenery of the Trent. We have clear running water in Trent right from Georgian bay down into lake Couchi-ching, into Pigeon lake, Clear lake, Stony lake, into lake Katchiwanooka, into Rice lake, and eventually down into the bay of Quinte, out through the Murray canal into lake Ontario, or going the other way along through Adolphus strait to Kingston. This is the most beautiful section of scenery in the whole country.
One of the most beautiful.

The most beautiful. I feel quite sure that if the Rideau is ever considered, then the Trent must be considered along with it. I may say that engineers from Pakistan have been through the district studying navigation, the dams and locks, in order to instal a navigation system in that country. They did see the Rideau, but because it was old-fashioned they turned to the Trent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Leeds, particularly when he was making a case for financial assistance to make possible an international peace garden down in the Thousand islands area. The project, as he outlined it, did seem most commendable. I should like to point out, in support of the hon. member for Brandon who has also mentioned the matter tonight, that before one tries to persuade the government to spend money on something that has not yet been started, perhaps we should get together and try to persuade the government not to discontinue a grant we have had for a number of years for the international peace garden on the southern boundary of Manitoba, south of the city of Brandon.

Supply-Resources and Development
To me it is a piece of irony, almost an affront, that in the estimates, the section with which we are now dealing, there should be this wording, "Appropriation not required for 1952-53, $15,000." When one turns over to page 440 to ascertain what it is for which the appropriation is not required, one finds it is a grant in aid of the development of the international peace garden in Manitoba. I know, Mr. Chairman, that is simply the technical language that is employed in the book of estimates to indicate that the estimate has been dropped. But I submit that the language is completely in error. The appropriation is required. We from Manitoba regret that the minister and the government have dropped it, despite all the representations that have been made, I believe by every member of parliament for Manitoba as well as by many organizations in our province that are interested in this project.
I hope that tonight the minister, when he heard an appeal for an international peace park on the St. Lawrence, had a feeling that his sins were catching up with him, and decided he had better go back to the treasury board and request the re-institution of this $15,000 grant for the international peace garden in Manitoba.

I should like to say a word with respect to this international peace garden. It is not only south of Brandon; it is also south of Boissevain which is in the riding I have the honour to represent. Like the other members from Manitoba, I have taken this matter up on several occasions, as well as having made a speech on it earlier in this session. Certainly, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the language in the estimates is most inappropriate. I am personally acquainted with a number of the officials of the international peace garden, and I can assure you they are having great difficulty in raising money to carry on the development in that area. We are very much disappointed that the minister has not seen his way clear to continuing this Worth-while grant. It was badly needed, not only for maintenance but for the development of what I think is one of the most worthy projects in this dominion.
The United States government have been making a fairly handsome grant towards the operation of this international peace garden, which is on the international boundary, just about half way across this country, approximately in the centre of North America. It is a very fine situation. I hope that the min-


ister will see fit to re-enact this grant which is so badly needed for this fine project.

I have just one question. I want to endorse what my Manitoba colleagues have said in connection with the peace garden. What I should like to ask the minister in connection with these parks is this. Has there been an extension of electricity into two or three more streets? Previously I drew the attention of the minister to the fact that they are using gasoline lamps and coal oil lamps there, and that this is a dangerous practice. You have electricity there. You could avoid a tremendous fire by extending electricity to a few more streets in order to accommodate the camps that are set up there.
Mr. Chairman, would you call it eleven o'clock? I wish to speak on the same subject.
